title: Weight and mass: what a scale really measures

summary.text: A bottle of water with holes in it stops leaking while it falls, though gravity still pulls it. Weight is the pull of gravity on a thing, measured in newtons. Mass is how much matter it has, measured in kilograms. We cannot sense gravity itself, only the push of the floor, a chair or water holding us up. So in a lift, in water or while falling we feel heavier or lighter, though gravity is the same.
summary.art: A child standing on a bathroom scale, with a long arrow from the child down to the centre of the Earth labelled 'pull', and a short arrow from the floor up into the child's feet labelled 'push'.

intro.hook: Hold a full water bottle on your flat palm and feel it press down. Now let it drop onto a cushion. While it was falling, nothing was holding it up. Was it still heavy?
intro.text: In 1907, Albert Einstein worked in an office in Bern, a city in Switzerland, checking other people's inventions. One day he had a sudden thought. A person falling freely from a roof would not feel their own weight. Years later, he called it the happiest thought of his life. Why would falling make weight disappear, and is the weight really gone? You will drop a leaking bottle of water to find out.
intro.art: A young Einstein at a wooden desk piled with papers, looking out of a window where a roofer is slipping off a roof, a thought bubble showing the man floating calmly in the air.

outcomes: I can say that weight is the pull of gravity on a thing, measured in newtons. I can say that mass is how much matter a thing has, measured in kilograms.
I can weigh things with a forcemeter. I hang the thing, wait until it is still, read the scale at eye level and write the unit. I can find the pattern: about 10 newtons for every kilogram on Earth.
I can explain that a scale or a forcemeter shows how hard it is holding a thing up. I can say that floors, chairs and water push back on us.

I can tell apart my weight, which is gravity's pull on me, from what a scale shows. I can say that the scale's number and my feeling of weight both come from the push holding me up. I can say which of them change in water, in a lift and while falling.
I can explain why astronauts float in the space station, even though gravity there is almost as strong as on the ground.
I can explain that weight changes from world to world but mass does not. I can say that mass is a form of energy.
I can say what scientists agree about weight and mass, and what they still do not know.

terms.meaning: The force by which everything attracts everything else. Attract means pull towards. Big things like the Earth attract very strongly. Small things attract too, but far too weakly to notice.
terms.example: Gravity pulls a mango down from the tree. It also holds the Moon near the Earth.
terms.art: A mango falling from a tree, and far above it the Moon, with faint arrows from both pointing towards the Earth.

terms.meaning: The pull of gravity on a thing. Weight is a force, so scientists measure it in newtons.
terms.example: A 1 kilogram packet of atta has a weight of about 10 newtons on Earth.
terms.art: A packet of atta hanging from a forcemeter, with a downward arrow labelled 10 newtons.

terms.meaning: How much matter a thing has. Matter is what things are made of: rice, water, air and you. Mass is measured in grams and kilograms. Your mass is the same everywhere, on Earth, on the Moon or in space.
terms.example: A 1 kilogram bag of rice is still 1 kilogram of rice on the Moon. Not one grain is lost.
terms.art: The same bag of rice on the Earth and on the Moon, labelled 1 kilogram both times.

terms.meaning: The unit for measuring mass. 1 kilogram is 1,000 grams. The short way to write it is kg.
terms.example: The water in a full one-litre bottle has a mass of about 1 kilogram.
terms.art: A full one-litre water bottle on a kitchen scale showing 1,000 grams.

terms.meaning: The unit for measuring force, and so for measuring weight. It is named after the scientist Isaac Newton. The short way to write it is N.
terms.example: A small apple has a weight of about 1 newton.
terms.art: A hand holding a small apple, with '1 N' written beside it.

terms.meaning: A tool that measures pushes and pulls. Inside is a spring. You hang a thing on its hook, and a pointer shows its weight in newtons. It is also called a newton meter or a spring balance.
terms.example: Hang a bag of dal on a forcemeter. The pointer shows how hard the Earth pulls it.
terms.art: A spring forcemeter hanging from a hook, a small bag of dal on its lower hook, the pointer at 5.

terms.meaning: The push from a floor, chair, bed or anything you rest on. It pushes back up as hard as you press down, so you do not sink in. Scientists call it the normal force.
terms.example: The floor is pushing up on your feet right now.
terms.art: A child standing on a floor, a small up arrow coming out of the floor into each foot.

terms.meaning: The push of water, or air, up on a thing that is in it. It makes things feel lighter in water.
terms.example: A heavy stone feels lighter when you lift it under water, in a bucket.
terms.art: A hand lifting a stone inside a bucket of water, with a small up arrow from the water under the stone.

terms.meaning: A tool for weighing. A bathroom scale measures how hard you press down on it. It turns that push into kilograms, using the Earth's pull. A forcemeter is a hanging scale.
terms.example: You stand on a bathroom scale at the doctor's clinic.
terms.art: A child standing on a bathroom scale with a dial.

terms.meaning: A small room that carries people up and down a tall building. In some countries it is called an elevator.
terms.example: The lift in a hospital or a block of flats.
terms.art: A lift with its doors open, a family inside, buttons with floor numbers.

terms.meaning: Falling with nothing holding you up, and almost no air slowing you. Things in free fall feel weightless.
terms.example: From the moment your feet leave the ground in a jump until you land, you are in free fall.
terms.art: A child at the top of a jump on a trampoline, hair floating up, a big smile.

terms.meaning: Having no feeling of weight, because nothing pushes on you to hold you up. Gravity is still pulling. There is just nothing pressing back on you.
terms.example: Astronauts in the space station float about, weightless.
terms.art: An astronaut floating upside down inside a space station, a pencil floating beside her.

terms.meaning: A big home for astronauts that goes round and round the Earth, above almost all of the air. The International Space Station goes round about 15 times a day.
terms.example: You can sometimes see the International Space Station from India, as a bright dot moving fast across the night sky.
terms.art: The International Space Station with its long solar panels, the curve of the blue Earth below.

terms.meaning: The path of something that keeps falling towards another thing, but moves sideways so fast that it keeps missing it.
terms.example: The Moon is in orbit round the Earth. The Earth is in orbit round the Sun.
terms.art: The Earth with the Moon moving round it, a dotted circle showing the path.

terms.meaning: The tiny building block that everything is made of. Atoms are far too small to see, even with an ordinary microscope.
terms.example: Your body, the floor and the air are all made of atoms.
terms.art: A zoom from a child's foot, to a speck of skin, to a cluster of tiny balls.

terms.meaning: An even tinier particle on the outside of every atom. Electrons repel other electrons, which means they push each other away. That push is what stops your feet sinking into the floor.
terms.example: When you press on a wall, the electrons of your hand and of the wall repel each other.
terms.art: Two atoms side by side, their fuzzy outer clouds of electrons pushing each other away.

terms.meaning: What it takes to make something move, warm up or change. Energy never disappears. It only changes from one kind into another.
terms.example: Food gives you energy to run. The Sun's light carries energy to the Earth.
terms.art: A child running, a plate of food, and the Sun, joined by little glowing arrows.

terms.meaning: A place in space where a huge amount of mass is squeezed into a tiny space. Its gravity is so strong that not even light can get out.
terms.example: There is a giant black hole at the centre of our galaxy, the Milky Way.
terms.art: A black circle in space surrounded by a glowing orange ring of hot gas.

terms.meaning: An old Sanskrit word for heaviness. Indian thinkers used it to explain why things fall. It comes from 'guru', which means heavy.
terms.example: Brahmagupta, an Indian astronomer, is reported to have written in 628 CE that the Earth attracts things towards it.
terms.art: An old palm-leaf manuscript with a drawing of a stone falling towards a round Earth.

terms.meaning: A Latin word meaning heaviness. Said of a person, it means a calm, serious way of being that makes people listen. It comes from 'gravis', which means heavy.
terms.example: A good teacher can quiet a noisy class just by standing still. People say she has gravitas.
terms.art: A calm teacher standing quietly while a noisy class turns to listen.

terms.meaning: Matter in space that we cannot see, but whose gravity we can measure. Scientists think there is about five times more of it than of ordinary matter.
terms.example: Stars at the edges of galaxies move too fast. Something unseen must be pulling them.
terms.art: A spiral galaxy with a faint, ghostly cloud drawn around it, labelled 'unseen mass'.

explanations.concept: Weight is the pull of gravity
explanations.definition: Weight is the pull of the Earth's gravity on a thing. It is a force, so it is measured in newtons.
explanations.description: Gravity is the force by which everything attracts everything else. The Earth is enormous, so its pull is strong. It pulls on every part of you, all the time, towards its centre. Add up the pull on all of you, and you get your weight. Because the pull is towards the centre, 'down' is not the same direction everywhere. For a child in Brazil, far round the Earth from India, down points a very different way. It still points to the centre of the Earth. The unit on measuring forces shows how a forcemeter works. This unit is about what it measures.
examples: A mango drops from a tree because the Earth pulls it.
A heavy school bag pulls down on your shoulders.
A plumb line, a stone on a string, always hangs straight down, towards the centre of the Earth. Builders use one to make walls straight.
explanations.art: The round Earth with children standing all round it, in India, Brazil and Antarctica, each with an arrow pointing to the Earth's centre.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the whole unit: what weight is.

explanations.definition: To weigh a thing with a forcemeter, hang it on the hook and wait until it stops bouncing. When it is still, the spring is pulling up exactly as hard as gravity pulls down. The pointer then shows the weight in newtons.
explanations.description: A forcemeter does not measure gravity directly. It measures the pull on its spring. When the thing hangs still, two forces balance. Gravity pulls it down, and the spring pulls it up just as hard. So the spring's pull tells us the weight. That is why you must wait until it is still. While it bounces, the number jumps about. Here is a handy pattern. On Earth, every 100 grams of anything weighs about 1 newton. So 1 kilogram, which is 1,000 grams, weighs about 10 newtons. A closer number is 9.8 newtons, but 10 is close enough for our sums.
examples: A 100 gram bar of soap reads about 1 newton.
A 500 gram packet of dal reads about 5 newtons.
A 1 litre bottle of water reads about 10 newtons.
explanations.art: Three forcemeters side by side: a soap bar at 1 newton, a dal packet at 5 newtons, a water bottle at 10 newtons.
explanations.context: How do you find out how heavy something is, in newtons? This card explains how to weigh things with a forcemeter, and a pattern to remember.

chart.title: Made-up example: the weight of bags of rice on a forcemeter
chart.note: Each extra 100 grams adds about 1 newton. A whole kilogram, 1,000 grams, weighs about 10 newtons.

explanations.concept: Mass and weight are not the same
explanations.definition: Mass is how much matter a thing has. Weight is how hard gravity pulls on that matter. Mass is measured in kilograms. Weight is measured in newtons.
explanations.description: In everyday talk, we say 'this bag weighs 2 kilos'. Shopkeepers say it, and that is fine. But scientists use two different words. The kilograms tell us how much rice is in the bag. That is its mass. The pull of the Earth on that rice is its weight. Take the bag to the Moon. Not a single grain of rice is lost. So the mass is the same. But the Moon pulls much more weakly. So the weight is about one sixth as big. A later card in this unit shows what you would weigh on other planets.
examples: A kilogram of cotton and a kilogram of iron have the same mass. On Earth, they also have the same weight. The cotton just takes up much more space.
An astronaut's mass is the same on the Moon. Her weight there is about one sixth of her weight on Earth.
If you eat a big lunch, your mass goes up a little, by the mass of the lunch.
explanations.art: Two scale pans balancing: a huge fluffy pile of cotton on one side and a small iron block on the other, both labelled 1 kilogram.
explanations.context: People often say 'weight' when they mean 'mass'. This card explains the difference.

explanations.definition: When you stand on the floor, the floor pushes up on you as hard as you press down on it. This push is called the support force, or the normal force.
explanations.description: Gravity pulls you towards the centre of the Earth. So why don't you sink through the floor? Because the floor pushes back. Zoom in, past anything a microscope can show, and you reach atoms. The outside of every atom is a cloud of electrons, and electrons repel each other. When your foot presses on the floor, the electrons of your foot and of the floor push each other apart. A hard floor hardly squashes at all, so it pushes back at once. A cushion is full of tiny pockets of air, so it squashes a little before it pushes back hard enough. Water flows out of the way, so your hand goes in. Jupiter, the biggest planet, is a giant ball of gas with no solid ground. A spacecraft falling into it just sinks into thicker and hotter gas, with no floor to stop it.
examples: Press your hand on a wall. The wall pushes back, so your hand stops.
Press your hand on a cushion. It sinks in a little, then the cushion pushes back.
Press your hand into a bucket of water. It goes right in, because the water flows aside.
explanations.art: Three panels: a hand pressed flat on a wall, a hand sinking into a cushion, a hand going into a bucket of water, with push-back arrows big, medium and small.
explanations.context: Gravity pulls you down all day. This card explains why you don't sink into the floor.

explanations.definition: The word weight is used in three ways. To a scientist, your weight is how hard gravity pulls you. What a scale shows is how hard it pushes up to hold you. Scientists call this your apparent weight, which means the weight it seems you have. How heavy you feel comes from that same push, pressing on your body.
explanations.description: Most of the time, all three are the same. Stand still on a bathroom scale on the floor. Gravity pulls you down with, say, 300 newtons. The scale pushes up with 300 newtons, and shows this as about 30 kilograms. And you feel your normal weight. But they can come apart. In a swimming pool, gravity still pulls you down just as hard. But the water pushes up on you too. So a scale under water would show less, and you feel light. In a lift that is starting to go up, the floor pushes up harder than usual. The scale shows more, and you feel heavier. When you fall freely, nothing holds you up at all. The scale would show zero, and you feel weightless. Gravity has not stopped. We feel our weight only through the push of the things that hold us up.
examples: Standing still on the ground: all three weights are the same.
Floating in a pool: gravity's pull is the same, but you feel almost weightless.
In a lift starting to go up: you feel heavier for a moment.
explanations.art: A child shown three times: on a scale on the floor (pull arrow and push arrow equal), floating in a pool (pull arrow, water push arrow), falling off a diving board (only the pull arrow).
explanations.context: Your weight can seem to change, even when gravity stays the same. This card explains three meanings of the word weight.

explanations.definition: Water pushes up on anything that is in it. This upward push is called upthrust. It makes things seem lighter in water, though gravity pulls them just as hard.
explanations.description: Hang a stone from a forcemeter. Then lower it into a bucket of water. The reading drops. Has the stone lost any of its mass? No. Lift it out and the reading goes back. Has gravity got weaker? No. The water is pushing up on the stone, so the spring has less to hold. The more of the stone that goes under the water, the bigger the push. This was worked out more than 2,200 years ago, by Archimedes, a thinker in Syracuse, a Greek city on the island of Sicily. In a pool, the same thing happens to you. If you breathe in and spread out, the water's push can hold up all of your weight. That is floating.
examples: A full mug feels much heavier once you lift it out of a bucket of water than while it is still under the water.
A big stone is easy to lift under water in a river, and suddenly heavy as it comes out.
Huge whales can grow so big because the sea holds up their weight.
explanations.art: A forcemeter holding a stone above a bucket reading 3, and the same stone inside the water reading 2, with a small up arrow from the water.
explanations.context: Why do things feel lighter in water? This card explains the push of water, using a stone on a forcemeter.

chart.title: Made-up example: a stone on a forcemeter, in air and in water
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what results can look like. Your numbers will be different.

explanations.concept: Heavier and lighter in a lift
explanations.definition: When a lift starts to go up, its floor must push you harder than usual to speed you up. So you feel heavier, and a scale shows more. When it starts to go down, the floor pushes less. So you feel lighter, and a scale shows less.
explanations.description: Gravity pulls on you just the same all through a lift ride. What changes is the push of the floor. To start you moving up, the floor has to push you up harder than gravity pulls you down. You feel that extra push in your knees. Once the lift is moving at a steady speed, the push goes back to normal. You feel normal, even though you are moving. When the lift slows down at the top, the floor pushes less. For a moment, you feel light. The same thing happens on a swing, a jhoola at a fair, or a bus going over a bump.
examples: A lift starting up: knees feel squashed, you feel heavy.
A lift slowing down at the top: your tummy feels floaty, you feel light.
A giant wheel at a mela going over the top: you feel lighter for a moment.
explanations.art: A family in a lift shown three times: starting up (knees bent, big up arrow from the floor), moving steadily (normal), slowing at the top (hair lifting, small up arrow).
explanations.context: Have you ever felt heavy or floaty in a lift? This card explains why, with readings from a forcemeter in a lift.

chart.title: Made-up example: a 1 kilogram bag on a forcemeter during a lift ride up
chart.note: Standing still: 10 newtons. The lift starts up: 11. Going up steadily: 10. Slowing down at the top: 9. Stopped: 10.

explanations.definition: When something falls freely, nothing holds it up. So it feels no weight, and a scale under it would read zero. Gravity is still pulling it. This is called free fall.
explanations.description: Hold a forcemeter with a weight hanging from it, then drop the whole thing onto a pillow. While it falls, the spring goes slack and the reading drops to zero. The weight and the forcemeter fall together, so the spring has nothing to hold. Poke holes near the bottom of a bottle of water and the water squirts out. Drop the bottle, and the squirting stops. The water and the bottle fall together, so the water no longer presses on the bottle. In 1907, Albert Einstein imagined a person falling from a roof. He realised they would feel no weight at all. He later called it the happiest thought of his life. It led him to a whole new picture of gravity.
examples: The floaty feeling in your tummy when you jump off a step.
A leaky bottle stops leaking while it falls.
A diver stepping off a high diving board feels weightless until she reaches the water.
explanations.art: A leaky bottle held still with three jets of water squirting out, and the same bottle falling with no water coming out.
explanations.context: What happens to weight when you fall? This card explains why falling things feel weightless.

explanations.concept: Astronauts float, but gravity is still there
explanations.definition: Astronauts float in the International Space Station because they and the station are falling together, all the time. Gravity up there is still about 90 out of every 100 parts as strong as on the ground.
explanations.description: The International Space Station flies about 400 kilometres above the Earth. That is about as far as driving from Chennai to Bengaluru, but straight up. The Earth's gravity there is only a little weaker than on the ground. So why do astronauts float? Because the station is falling. It also moves sideways incredibly fast, about 7.7 kilometres every second. As it falls, the round Earth curves away below it. So it keeps falling, and keeps missing. It goes round the Earth about 15 times every day. Everything inside falls together. Nothing pushes on the astronauts, so they feel weightless. The next unit, on orbits, explains this falling round and missing.
examples: In 2007, Sunita Williams, an astronaut whose father came from Gujarat, ran the Boston Marathon on a treadmill in the space station. Stretchy cords pulled her down onto the treadmill, so her feet had something to push on.
Kalpana Chawla, from Karnal in Haryana, flew in space in 1997. She became the first woman of Indian origin in space.
Astronauts drink from pouches with straws. Water will not pour out of a glass up there. It floats out in wobbly balls.
explanations.art: Inside the space station, an astronaut running on a treadmill held down by stretchy cords on her shoulders, a window showing the Earth below.
explanations.context: Many people think there is no gravity in space. This card explains why astronauts really float.

explanations.definition: How hard a world pulls on you depends on its mass, and on how far you are from its centre. So the same thing weighs more on some worlds and less on others. Its mass stays the same.
explanations.description: The Moon has much less mass than the Earth. So it pulls you with only about one sixth of the Earth's pull. Astronauts on the Moon bounced about easily in their heavy suits. Jupiter has more than 300 times the Earth's mass. But it is also huge, so its cloud tops are far from its centre. There, you would weigh about two and a half times your Earth weight. The Sun is far bigger again. At its surface, you would weigh about 28 times as much. You could not stand on Jupiter or the Sun, of course. Neither has solid ground. A black hole squeezes a huge mass into a tiny space. Near it, the pull would be strong enough to stretch you long and thin, like a noodle.
examples: A child with a mass of 30 kilograms weighs about 300 newtons on Earth, and about 50 newtons on the Moon.
On Mars, the same child would weigh a little more than a third of their Earth weight.
Your mass, 30 kilograms, would be the same in every one of these places.
explanations.art: The same child jumping on the Moon (very high), the Earth (normal) and Jupiter's clouds (barely off the ground), with mass 30 kg written beside each.
explanations.context: Would you weigh the same on the Moon or the Sun? This card shows how weight changes from world to world, while mass stays the same.

chart.title: The weight of a child with a mass of 30 kilograms, in different places
chart.note: The child's mass is 30 kilograms everywhere. Only the pull changes. The Sun and Jupiter have no ground to stand on, so these are 'if you could stand there' numbers.

explanations.concept: Gravity is a tiny bit different all over the Earth
explanations.definition: The Earth's pull is not exactly the same everywhere. It is a little weaker at the equator than at the North and South Poles. It is a little weaker on high mountains, and a little stronger over heavy rock.
explanations.description: The Earth spins, and it bulges a little round its middle, the equator. So at the equator you are a bit further from the centre, and the spin also flings you outwards a little. Together, these make you weigh about half a percent less than at the poles. That is about half a newton less for every 10 kilograms. On top of a high mountain, you are further from the centre too, so you weigh very slightly less. Heavy rock deep under the ground pulls a tiny bit harder. Scientists map all these tiny differences. Gladys West, a mathematician in the United States, worked for years on computer models of the Earth's exact shape. Her work helped GPS, the system that tells phones where they are, to find places accurately. Satellites can even measure underground water by its pull. In 2009, scientists used two such satellites, called GRACE, to show that underground water in north-western India was being used up fast.
examples: A 30 kilogram child weighs about 293 newtons near the equator, and about 295 newtons near the North Pole.
On top of Mount Everest, you would weigh very slightly less than in Mumbai.
Your phone's map uses the Earth's exact shape to show where you are.
explanations.art: A slightly squashed Earth, bulging at the equator, with a child weighing a little less at the equator and a little more at the pole.
explanations.context: Is your weight the same in every place on Earth? This card is about the tiny differences, and the scientists who measure them.

explanations.concept: Mass is a form of energy
explanations.definition: Mass and energy are two forms of the same thing. Albert Einstein showed this in 1905, with his famous rule E = mc². A little mass holds a huge amount of energy.
explanations.description: Mass can turn into energy, and energy has mass. The Sun shines by turning a little of its mass into light. It loses about 4 million tonnes of mass every second, and it still has plenty left. Zoom inside one of your atoms. In its middle are tiny particles called protons and neutrons. Inside those are even tinier particles called quarks. They move about with enormous energy, held together by a very strong force. Most of your mass is really this energy. Even a cup of hot chai has a teeny bit more mass than the same cup when it is cold. The extra energy of heat adds mass, but far too little to weigh. Light has no mass at all. But it has energy, so gravity still bends its path. Energy, not only mass, is what gravity works on.
examples: The Sun turns about 4 million tonnes of its mass into light and heat every second.
In 1919, scientists saw starlight bend as it passed close to the Sun, during an eclipse.
Nuclear power stations, like the one at Tarapur in Maharashtra, turn a tiny bit of mass into a lot of energy.
explanations.art: A zoom into a child's hand: skin, an atom, its centre, and three glowing quarks zooming inside, labelled 'most of your mass is this energy'.
explanations.context: This card goes deep, to what mass really is. It explains Einstein's famous discovery that mass is a kind of energy.

explanations.concept: Why gravity pulls a heavy thing harder
explanations.description: Mass does two jobs. It is what gravity pulls on. A big mass gets a big pull. Mass is also what makes a thing hard to push. A full almirah is harder to get moving than an empty one. Here is the strange part. These two kinds of mass are always exactly equal, for every thing ever tested. Scientists have checked this very carefully. In 2022, a satellite called MICROSCOPE finished testing it more precisely than ever before. No difference was found. Nobody knows why the two are equal. Einstein did not try to explain it. He made it the starting point of his whole picture of gravity. The Things fall unit shows one result of this: heavy and light things fall together.
examples: A full trolley needs a bigger push to start, and it also weighs more.
A heavy cricket ball and a light tennis ball, dropped together, land together.

perspectives.who: Isaac Newton, in 1687, and most scientists after him
perspectives.explanation: The two kinds of mass are equal. Newton tested it with pendulums made of different materials. It is a fact of nature that we measure, but cannot yet explain.

They are equal because gravity and speeding up are really the same thing. A person in a closed box cannot tell if they are standing on Earth or speeding up in a rocket. This idea became his theory of gravity.

explanations.art: A child pushing a full trolley, and the same trolley hanging from a giant forcemeter, with a question mark joining them.
explanations.context: This card is about a deep puzzle. Mass makes things heavy, and mass makes things hard to push. Why are these always exactly the same?

explanations.description: We can measure weight very well. But what is gravity itself? This is one of the biggest questions in science. Here are the main ideas.
examples: A heavy ball on a stretched bedsheet makes a dip. Marbles rolled nearby curve towards it.
A clock on a high mountain ticks a tiny bit faster than one at sea level. Einstein's picture of gravity predicted this, and very careful clocks show it.

perspectives.who: Isaac Newton, an English scientist, in 1687
perspectives.explanation: Every mass pulls every other mass. The pull is bigger for bigger masses, and smaller when they are further apart. Newton said he did not know how the pull reaches across empty space.

perspectives.who: Albert Einstein, a German-born scientist, in 1915
perspectives.explanation: Nothing is really pulling at all. Mass and energy bend space and time around them, like a heavy ball denting a stretched sheet. Things move along the bend, and that is what we see as falling. This idea has passed every test so far.

Einstein's idea works for planets and stars. But it does not fit with quantum physics, the science of the very tiniest things. Some think gravity is carried by a tiny particle called a graviton. Nobody has ever found one. Others think gravity grows out of something deeper. Nobody knows yet.

explanations.art: A stretched bedsheet held by four children, a heavy ball making a deep dip, marbles curving towards it.
explanations.context: Weight is the pull of gravity. This card asks a harder question: what is gravity itself? Scientists still argue about it.

explanations.description: Everything has mass. But where does mass come from? Scientists have found part of the answer, and some of it is still a mystery.
examples: Electrons are so light that about 1,800 of them would have the mass of one proton.
In 2012, scientists at a giant machine near Geneva, in Europe, found a new tiny particle called the Higgs boson.

perspectives.who: Peter Higgs and others, in 1964, and the scientists of CERN, in 2012
perspectives.explanation: Space is filled with something invisible called the Higgs field. Tiny particles like electrons and quarks get their own small mass from it. In 2012, the Higgs boson was found at CERN, a laboratory near Geneva. It showed the field is real.
The Higgs field gives only a small part of your mass. Most of it comes from the energy of quarks moving inside protons and neutrons, and of the strong force that holds them together.
Why does each tiny particle have exactly the mass it has? Why is the electron so light? Nobody knows. It is an open question.

explanations.art: A crowded room where one person glides through easily and another is slowed by everyone gathering round them, labelled 'the Higgs field idea'.
explanations.context: Weight comes from mass. This card asks where mass itself comes from, which scientists have only partly worked out.

explanations.concept: Living things are built for weight
explanations.description: Every living thing on Earth grew up with gravity pulling on it. Our bones grow strong because they carry our weight every day. In the space station, nothing presses on astronauts' bones, so they get weaker. The hip bones can lose about 1 to 1.5 parts in every 100 each month. So astronauts exercise for about two hours every day. Plants know which way is down too. Lay a seedling on its side, and its root bends to grow downwards again. How does a plant feel which way is down? Most scientists have one main idea, but the full answer is still being studied.
examples: Astronauts coming back from months in space often need help to walk at first.
A seed planted upside down still sends its root down and its shoot up.

perspectives.who: Gottlieb Haberlandt and Bohumil Němec, two scientists, in 1900, and most scientists today
perspectives.explanation: Special cells near the root tip hold tiny heavy grains of starch. The grains sink to the bottom of each cell, like sand in a jar of water. The cell feels where they settle, and so it knows which way is down.
Plants with no starch grains can still sense down, though more slowly. So there may be other ways too, like feeling the weight of the whole cell pressing on its walls.

explanations.art: A sideways seedling whose root has bent to grow down, and a zoom into a root-tip cell with tiny grains settled at the bottom.
explanations.context: Living things grew up with gravity. This card looks at how bones and plants use weight, and what scientists still do not know.

explanations.description: People have wondered about heaviness for thousands of years, in many places. Who first understood weight? It depends on what you count.
examples: Ancient Indian thinkers used the word gurutva, heaviness, to explain falling.
Isaac Newton's book Principia, in 1687, gave the rule for how gravity's pull changes with distance.

perspectives.who: Kanada, an Indian thinker of the Vaisheshika school, more than 2,000 years ago
perspectives.explanation: Things fall because of gurutva, a heaviness inside them.

perspectives.who: Aristotle, a Greek thinker, about 2,350 years ago
perspectives.explanation: Heavy things move down to their natural place, the centre of the world. He thought heavy things fall faster. That part was wrong.

perspectives.who: Brahmagupta in 628 CE, and Bhaskara II in the 1100s, two Indian astronomers
perspectives.explanation: The Earth attracts things towards itself, just as it is the nature of water to flow. Bhaskara II wrote of the Earth's power of attraction.

perspectives.who: Al-Khazini, a scientist in Merv, in the 1100s
perspectives.explanation: In his Book of the Balance of Wisdom, he studied weighing very carefully. Historians say he wrote that a thing's heaviness changes with its distance from the centre of the Earth.
Every mass pulls every other mass, with a rule for how strong the pull is. The same pull drops an apple and holds the Moon. Historians agree this mathematical law was new.

explanations.art: A row of thinkers from different times and places, Kanada, Aristotle, Brahmagupta, al-Khazini and Newton, each holding a falling stone.
explanations.context: This card is about the long history of ideas about heaviness, in India, Greece, Persia and England.

agreed.text: Weight is the pull of gravity on a thing. It is a force, measured in newtons.
agreed.evidence: Hang a thing on a forcemeter, and the spring stretches, because gravity pulls the thing down. Twice the mass stretches it twice as far. On the Moon, where the pull is about one sixth as strong, Apollo astronauts in heavy suits hopped about easily.

agreed.text: Mass stays the same wherever a thing goes. Weight changes with the pull of the place.
agreed.evidence: A pan balance compares one mass with another, so it gives the same answer on a high mountain or at sea level. A forcemeter measures the pull, so careful ones read very slightly less on a high mountain.

agreed.text: A scale measures how hard it pushes to hold a thing up, not gravity directly.
agreed.evidence: The same person gives different readings in a lift, in water and while falling, though the Earth's pull on them hardly changes.

agreed.text: Astronauts in the space station float because they are falling, not because gravity has gone.
agreed.evidence: Measurements and sums both agree. The Earth's gravity at the station is about 90 out of every 100 parts as strong as on the ground. If gravity were gone, the station would fly off in a straight line instead of going round the Earth.

agreed.text: Mass is a form of energy.
agreed.evidence: Einstein's rule E = mc² has been tested in many ways. In nuclear power stations, the atoms that are left after splitting have slightly less mass than at the start. The missing mass comes out as energy. The Sun shines in a similar way.

agreed.text: The Earth's pull is slightly different from place to place.
agreed.evidence: Very sensitive instruments, on the ground and on satellites, measure it everywhere. It is about half a percent weaker at the equator than at the poles.

challenging.claim: There is no gravity in space. That is why astronauts float.
challenging.who: Many people, and some films and cartoons
challenging.for: Astronauts really do float. And far from every planet and star, gravity is very weak.
challenging.against: The space station is only about 400 kilometres up. The Earth's gravity there is still about 90 out of every 100 parts as strong as on the ground. Gravity keeps the station going round the Earth. Astronauts float because they are falling together with the station.
challenging.context: This card is about a very common idea: that astronauts float because space has no gravity.

challenging.claim: When you feel lighter, gravity has become weaker.
challenging.who: A common way of thinking, for example in a pool or a lift
challenging.for: We really do feel lighter in water, and when a lift starts going down.
challenging.against: Gravity pulls you just as hard in the pool and in the lift. What changes is the push holding you up. Water pushes up on you. A lift's floor pushes less as it starts down. What we feel is never gravity itself, only the things that push back on us.
challenging.context: This card is about why we sometimes feel lighter or heavier, and whether gravity really changes.

challenging.for: Scientists measure weight in newtons, and mass in kilograms. So strictly, a 30 kilogram child has a weight of about 300 newtons.
challenging.against: In everyday life, almost everyone says it, and on Earth it causes no problems. Even the government's weights and measures rules use kilograms for shops. Scientists just need to be careful which one they mean.
challenging.context: This card is about the words we use for weight and mass, and whether everyday talk is wrong.

challenging.claim: Light has no mass, so gravity cannot pull on it.
challenging.who: Many people, and some scientists before 1919
challenging.for: Light really does have no mass. Newton's rule for gravity is about masses pulling masses.
challenging.against: In 1919, during a total eclipse of the Sun, astronomers photographed stars close to the Sun. Their light had been bent by the Sun's gravity, by about the amount Einstein had predicted. Gravity works on energy, and light carries energy. Today, telescopes see galaxies bent into rings by gravity.
challenging.context: This card asks whether gravity can pull on light, which has no mass at all.

challenging.claim: Isaac Newton discovered gravity when an apple fell on his head.
challenging.for: Newton himself, as an old man, told friends that watching an apple fall got him thinking about gravity.
challenging.against: Nobody recorded the apple hitting his head. People everywhere already knew things fall. Brahmagupta, an Indian astronomer, wrote in 628 CE that the Earth attracts things. Newton's real discovery, in 1687, was the mathematical law. It showed that one pull drops apples and holds the Moon.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous story of how gravity was discovered, and what Newton really did.

challenging.claim: Gravity is a force, just like a push or a pull from your hand.
challenging.who: Isaac Newton's picture, still used in most schoolbooks
challenging.for: Newton's picture works brilliantly. It is used to send spacecraft to the Moon and Mars, like India's Chandrayaan missions.
challenging.against: Albert Einstein, in 1915, said gravity is not really a pull. Mass bends space and time, and things fall along the bend. Both pictures are used. Einstein's is more exact near huge masses.
challenging.context: This card asks whether gravity is really a force, or something stranger.

challenging.who: Some scientists wondered about this for many years
challenging.for: Antimatter is a strange mirror version of ordinary matter. Nobody had ever measured which way it falls.
challenging.against: In 2023, scientists at CERN, near Geneva, finally dropped atoms of anti-hydrogen. They fell downwards, like ordinary atoms.
challenging.context: Antimatter is a strange mirror version of the matter we are made of. This card is about whether gravity pulls it down.

big_questions.q: If you feel no weight while you are falling, is your weight still there?
big_questions.hint: Gravity is still pulling. What has gone away is the push that holds you up.

big_questions.q: Why can't you feel gravity itself, only the floor pushing back?
big_questions.hint: Gravity pulls every part of you along together, so no part presses on another. A floor pushes only on your feet.

big_questions.q: Is there anywhere in the universe with no gravity at all?
big_questions.hint: Every star and planet pulls, even from very far away. Can you ever get so far that nothing pulls you?

big_questions.q: If the Earth pulls you, do you pull the Earth too? Why doesn't the Earth move towards you?
big_questions.hint: Gravity pulls both ways. Think about how much more mass the Earth has than you.

big_questions.q: On the Moon you would weigh less, but you would still be you. So what is the real you: your weight, your mass, or something else?
big_questions.hint: Think about what stays the same when you travel, and what changes.

big_questions.q: You feel your weight only through the push of the floor, a chair or the water. If nothing touched you at all, how could you tell that you had weight?
big_questions.hint: Think about the falling bottle, and the astronauts. What could you measure instead of a push?

big_questions.q: The Sanskrit word guru means heavy, and a guru is a teacher. The Latin word gravitas means weight, and a person with gravitas makes people listen. Why do people link heaviness with wisdom?
big_questions.hint: Is it a good thing to be 'heavy' in this way? Can a child have gravitas?

big_questions.q: Gravity holds the whole universe together, but it never lets you fly. Is gravity good or bad?
big_questions.hint: The Gravity song for this topic asks this exact question. What would happen if gravity switched off for one minute?

big_questions.q: Most of your mass is really the energy of tiny particles moving inside your atoms. So are you made of matter, or of energy?
big_questions.hint: Einstein showed mass and energy are two forms of the same thing.

big_questions.q: Stars at the edges of galaxies move as if pulled by mass that nobody can see. Should we trust that something is there if we can only measure it, and never see it?
big_questions.hint: You cannot see gravity either. How do you know it is there?

big_questions.q: Astronauts' bones get weaker without weight to carry. How might a bone tell how much weight it is carrying?
big_questions.hint: Bone is alive. Its cells sense being squeezed, and build more bone where the squeeze is.

big_questions.q: If you dug a tunnel right through the Earth and jumped in, what would you weigh at the very centre?
big_questions.hint: At the centre, the Earth is all around you, pulling in every direction at once.

story.title: What the Pond Holds
story.note: Made up. Gauri, her mother Sunaina, her uncle Bholu Mama and the pond are imagined. Makhana, the fox nut, really is grown in ponds in Mithila, in north Bihar, around Darbhanga and Madhubani. Harvesters really do dive to gather the seeds from the muddy bottom, and its leaves really can grow more than a metre across. The physics is true: water pushes up on whatever is in it, and arms and a head held out of the water get no help from it.
text: I am a pond in Mithila, in the north of Bihar. I am not deep, and I am not grand. I am brown in the monsoon and green in the winter. But I am old, and I hold many things.

I hold the makhana plants. Their leaves lie flat on my skin, round and wrinkled, some of them wider than a child is tall. Frogs sit on them like kings on carpets. Under the leaves, the plants drop their seeds into my mud. And every year, when the seeds are ready, the people come down my steps and dive.

Sunaina was the best diver of them all. She would slip under me like a fish, without a splash, and come up with her hands full of black seeds and grey mud. Her brother, Bholu Mama, stood on the bank with a sack and a hanging spring balance on a bamboo pole. He weighed each sack before it went to the trader.
Sunaina's daughter, Gauri, was eight years old, and she would not come in.
She sat on my top step every morning, with her knees under her chin. 'I'll sink,' she said, whenever her mother called. 'Like a stone. I'm too heavy.'
'You are not a stone,' Sunaina said. 'Breathe in, and you will float.'
'Not me,' said Gauri.

One hot afternoon, a sack of wet seeds slipped off the bank. It slid into my shallows, still hanging from the hook of Bholu Mama's balance. He grabbed the pole before it fell. Gauri watched the needle on the dial. As the sack sank into me, the needle crept back, back, back towards zero.
'The pond is stealing its weight!' Gauri cried.

Bholu Mama laughed and hauled the sack out. Water poured from it, and the needle swung all the way back. 'The pond never steals anything,' he said. 'It only holds.' Gauri frowned at me for a long time after that.
The next morning, she let her mother lead her down my steps. One step, two steps, three. My water reached her knees, then her waist. She was shivering, though the sun was warm.
'Lie back,' said Sunaina. 'I have your back. Let the water have you.'

Gauri leaned back. My cold water touched her neck and crept towards her ears. And then she panicked. She threw her arms up into the air, as if to save them. She pulled her head up high. She kicked hard at me, again and again. And she sank, just as she had said she would. She came up coughing, her eyes stinging, and ran up my steps without looking back.

I felt sorry, the way old ponds do. I had wanted to hold her. But a pond can only hold what is in it. Her arms were in the air, and her head was in the air. I could push on the part of her that was in me. I could not push on the rest. So she had given me only a little of herself to hold, and the rest of her was pulled down.

That night, Gauri lay awake on her charpai. She thought about the sack on the hook, and the needle creeping back to zero. The sack had not been lighter. Bholu Mama said so. The water had been holding it up from underneath. She thought about the makhana leaves, flat and wide on my skin. Some were wider than she was tall. Yet they never sank.
In the morning there was mist on me, so thick the frogs were only voices. Gauri came down my steps alone. Her mother was already in the water, waiting quietly by the third step.
'Again?' said Sunaina.
'Again,' said Gauri.

This time she did not hurry. She took a long, deep breath, until her chest was round and full. She let her ears go under, though she hated it. And she did a strange thing. She laid her arms out wide on my water, flat, like the leaves of the makhana. She did not keep a single part of herself out of me.
Sunaina's hand was under her back. Then it was a finger. Then it was gone.
And I held her. All of her.

Understand this. I did not take away her weight. Nothing on this Earth can do that. The Earth pulled her down exactly as hard as it pulls the herons and the stones in my mud. But all of her was in me now. So I could push up on all of her, and my push was enough. Her weight was still there. It was just being carried, the way her mother carried her when she was small.
Gauri lay on top of me and looked up into the mist. A heron flew over, slow and grey. Her ears were full of my quiet sounds. She felt as light as a makhana leaf.
'Amma,' she whispered, without moving. 'I'm floating.'
'I know,' said Sunaina. Her eyes were wet, and it was not only from me.
Bholu Mama came down to the bank with his sack and his pole. He saw the small girl lying on the water with her arms out wide. He did not shout. He just stood still and smiled.

These days, Gauri dives for seeds beside her mother. She slips under me without a splash. When she comes up for air, she lies back for a moment, arms wide, and lets me carry her. She gives me all of herself. And I give it all back.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Gauri does not float because she gets lighter. The Earth pulls her just as hard in the pond. She floats because the water pushes up on every part of her that is under it. When she panics and holds her arms and head up in the air, the water cannot push on those parts, so its push is too small and she sinks. When she breathes in, lies back and spreads out like the makhana leaf, all of her is in the water. Now its push can carry all her weight. The sack on the spring balance shows the same thing: the needle drops not because the sack lost weight, but because the water was holding part of it up. We feel weight only through what holds us.
ask: When the sack slipped into the pond, the needle went back towards zero. Had the sack really got lighter?
Why did Gauri sink the first time, when she held her arms and head up in the air?
What did Gauri copy from the makhana leaves the second time?
The pond says, 'I did not take away her weight.' What did it do instead?
When you float in a pool, what holds you up? What holds you up when you lie on your bed?
art: A brown village pond in Mithila covered with giant round makhana leaves, frogs sitting on them, divers' heads bobbing between.
Bholu Mama on the bank holding a bamboo pole with a hanging spring balance and a dripping sack, its hook dipped into the water.
Gauri thrashing in the water with her arms thrown up in the air, her mother reaching for her.
Gauri floating on her back in the morning mist, arms spread wide like a leaf, a heron flying over.
Years later, Gauri and her mother diving side by side among the makhana leaves.

printables.title: 4 counters, one for each player, and one dice

rules: Before you start, each player does two challenge cards and earns two force cards.
Put your counter on EARTH. Take turns to roll the dice and move forward.
If you land on a gravity event, you must do what it says. But you can stop it by playing a force card that beats it. You must say how that force fights gravity.
If you land on a star, do any challenge card to earn a new force card.
If you land on a forward square, move forward as it says.
The first player to reach SPACE wins. But to win, they must answer one question. Is gravity still pulling you in space?

flow.do: 1. Lay out the board. 2. Shuffle the force cards and challenge cards into two piles. 3. Each player does two challenge cards and takes the force cards they earn.
flow.say: We're going to race from the Earth into space. Gravity will try to pull us back. To fight it, we need force cards. You earn them by doing small challenges.
flow.kid: Lay out the board. Do two challenge cards. Each one earns you a force card. You will need them to fight gravity!
flow.context: This is the first step of Escape Gravity, the founder's board game. Players race from the Earth to Space, and use force cards to fight gravity's pull.

flow.do: Play one practice turn together. Put a counter on square 5, Splashdown, and decide which card beats it.
flow.say: Practice turn. You've fallen into a lake, square 5. Which force card saves you, and why?
flow.kid: Practice turn! You fell into a lake. Which force card saves you? Tap your answer.

check.q: Splashdown: you fall into a lake. Which force card saves you?
options: Nothing can, gravity is gone in water
check.why: In this game moment, UPTHRUST wins. Water pushes up on anything in it, so it can hold up a floating person. Gravity is still pulling in the lake, just as hard as on land. Picking 'gravity is gone in water' is a very common idea, because we feel so light there. The lightness comes from the water's push, not from less gravity.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to roll and move. 2. On a gravity event, the player may play a force card and explain it. 3. On a star, they do a challenge card.
flow.say: When you play a force card, tell us how it fights gravity. A good explanation saves you.
flow.kid: Roll and move. Gravity event? Play a force card. Say how it fights gravity. Star? Do a challenge and earn a card.

ask.q: Why does SUPPORT FORCE beat the Rotten Plank?
good: A strong floor pushes back up on me, so I don't fall through.
The floor's electrons repel the electrons of my feet.

ask.q: Why does only SIDEWAYS SPEED beat the black hole?
good: If you go sideways fast enough, you fall round it instead of into it.
Going sideways fast is the only way to keep falling round it and missing.

flow.parent: Accept any explanation that names a push or pull against gravity. On the Lift Going Up square, STEADY SPEED works because the extra heavy feeling comes only while the lift speeds up. Once it moves steadily, you feel normal again. On Trampoline, the stretched mat pushes up harder than your weight, so you shoot up.

flow.do: When someone reaches SPACE, ask them the winning question before they win.
flow.say: You made it to space! Here's your last question. Is the Earth's gravity still pulling you up here?
flow.kid: You reached SPACE! One last question. Is gravity still pulling you? Say why.

check.q: You reached space, 400 kilometres up, where the space station flies. Is the Earth's gravity still pulling you?
options: Yes, almost as strongly as on the ground
No, there is no gravity in space
Only a tiny bit, about one hundredth
check.why: In this game, the winner has to know this. At the height of the space station, gravity is still about 90 out of every 100 parts as strong as on the ground. Astronauts float because they are falling together with their station. Picking 'no gravity in space' is the most common mix-up of all, because astronauts float.

flow.do: Look back at the force cards together.
flow.say: Which force card did you use most? Which force fights gravity most often in real life?
flow.kid: Which force card did you use most? Which force fights gravity for you all day long?
flow.think: Right now, something is pushing you up so that gravity does not pull you through the floor. What is it?

games.title: Pull Cards: who pulls hardest?
games.context: This is a card game made from the founder's element cards. Each card is a thing in the universe, from a dust speck to a giant black hole. Its mass and energy are shown as arrows. Players compare pulls and guess what would happen to a person there.

printables.title: 16 element cards to cut out
items: A DUST SPECK. Mass: a tiny dot. Pull: far too small to feel.
YOU. Mass: about 30 kilograms. Pull: tiny, but real. You pull the Earth too!
AN ELEPHANT. Mass: about 5,000 kilograms. Pull: still far too small to feel.
THE HIMALAYAS. Mass: huge. Pull: a plumb line near the mountains leans very slightly towards them.
A MOUNTAIN OF GRANITE. Mass: big. Heavy rock pulls a tiny bit harder.
QUICKSAND. Mass: medium. Wet sand gives way under your feet, so you sink in.
THE OCEAN. Mass: big. It pushes you up, so you feel light.
AN ASTEROID. Mass: a mountain's worth. Pull: so weak one jump could launch you into space.
THE MOON. Mass: ↑↑. Your weight: about one sixth of Earth's.
MARS. Mass: ↑↑. Your weight: a bit more than one third of Earth's.
THE EARTH. Mass: ↑↑↑. Your weight: about 300 newtons, if your mass is 30 kilograms.
JUPITER. Mass: ↑↑↑↑. No ground. Your weight at the cloud tops: about two and a half times Earth's.
THE SUN. Mass: ↑↑↑↑↑. No ground. Your weight at the surface: about 28 times Earth's.
A SMALL BLACK HOLE. Mass: ten Suns, squeezed tiny. Its pull would stretch you like a noodle.
A GIANT BLACK HOLE. Mass: millions of Suns. Even light cannot get out.
LIGHT. Mass: zero. Energy: yes! Gravity still bends its path.

printables.title: 8 outcome cards
items: You land on solid ground. It pushes back. You stand.
You sink, because nothing pushes back hard enough.
You float, because water holds you up.
You bounce very high, because the pull is weak.
You fall round and round in orbit, falling and missing.
You are squashed flat by a huge pull.
You hardly notice any pull at all.
Your path bends, but you keep going.

printables.title: Pull score sheet
items: Round
Player 1 card
Player 2 card
Who pulls harder?
Outcome card played
Points

rules: Shuffle the element cards. Deal 4 to each player. Spread the outcome cards face up in the middle.
Each round, everyone puts down one element card at the same time.
The card with the strongest pull on a person wins the round and scores 1 point. Mass arrows help you decide. More mass close by means more pull.
Then each player picks the outcome card that fits their own card. A right outcome scores 1 extra point.
LIGHT is special. It always loses on pull, but if you can explain why gravity bends it, you score 2 points.
After 4 rounds, the player with the most points wins.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Shuffle the element cards and deal 4 to each player. 3. Spread the outcome cards face up.
flow.say: Every card is a thing in the universe. The more mass something has, the harder it pulls. Let's see who pulls hardest.
flow.kid: Get 4 element cards each. Look at the mass arrows. More arrows means more mass. More mass means a bigger pull.
flow.context: This is the first step of Pull Cards. It is a card game about how hard different things in the universe pull, from a dust speck to a black hole.

flow.do: Play a practice round with THE MOON and THE EARTH.
flow.say: Practice round. The Moon against the Earth. Which pulls you harder? And which outcome card fits the Moon?
flow.kid: Practice! The Moon against the Earth. Which one pulls you harder? Tap it.

check.q: Which pulls you harder when you stand on it, the Moon or the Earth?
check.why: In this round, the Earth wins. It has much more mass than the Moon, so it pulls much harder. On the Moon you weigh about one sixth as much, so you can bounce very high. Picking 'the same' usually means thinking gravity is one fixed thing everywhere. It changes with the mass of the world.

flow.do: 1. Play 4 rounds. 2. Each round, everyone plays one card. 3. Decide the winner, then each player picks an outcome card.
flow.say: Put your cards down together. Who pulls hardest? Now, what would happen to a person on your card?
flow.kid: Put down a card. Who pulls hardest? Now pick the outcome that fits your card. What would happen to you there?
flow.parent: Good matches: Jupiter and the Sun, 'you sink' (no ground). The ocean, 'you float'. The asteroid and the Moon, 'you bounce very high'. Light, 'your path bends'. Quicksand, 'you sink', but only to about your waist, because quicksand is thicker than water and holds you up there. A black hole is tricky: up close, 'squashed' or stretched. Far away and moving sideways fast, 'falling round in orbit'.

ask.q: The Sun has far more mass than Jupiter. Why can't you stand on either of them?
good: They are made of gas, with no solid ground.
Nothing would push back, so you would keep sinking.

flow.do: End the game by talking about the LIGHT card.
flow.say: Light has no mass at all. So why does gravity still bend it?
flow.kid: Light has no mass. But gravity still bends it! Why do you think that is?
flow.parent: Einstein showed that energy, not only mass, is what gravity works on. Light carries energy. In 1919, astronomers saw starlight bend as it passed close to the Sun during an eclipse.
flow.think: If light has no mass but gravity still bends it, is gravity really about mass at all?

experiments.title: How hard does a kilogram pull?
experiments.question: If we weigh more and more rice on a forcemeter, is there a pattern between grams and newtons?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. If 100 grams of rice reads 1 newton, what will 500 grams read? What will a whole kilogram read? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same forcemeter and the same kind of thin plastic bag every time. Check the pointer is at zero with the empty bag. Wait until the bag stops bouncing before you read. Change only the amount of rice.
results_table: Mass of rice (grams), from the kitchen scale

materials.item: a forcemeter that measures up to 10 or 20 newtons
a kitchen scale, or packets with the mass printed on them (a 100 gram soap, a 500 gram dal packet, a 1 kilogram atta packet)
rice or dal, about 1 kilogram, and a thin plastic bag with handles
a hook or a door handle to hang the forcemeter from, and a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Hang the forcemeter from something steady. Keep your face away from the hook in case the bag slips.

schedule.what: Weigh 100, 200, 300, 500 and 1,000 grams of rice on the forcemeter. Find the pattern and draw a line graph.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a line graph. Put grams along the bottom and newtons up the side. Join the dots.
experiments.context: In this experiment you weigh bags of rice on a forcemeter, a spring tool that measures weight in newtons. You look for a pattern between grams and newtons.

flow.do: 1. Hang the forcemeter from a hook or a door handle. 2. Hang the empty plastic bag on its hook. 3. Check the pointer is at zero. If it is not, turn the zero screw at the top until it is.
flow.say: A forcemeter measures how hard something pulls. First we make sure it reads zero with just the empty bag. Otherwise every number will be wrong.
flow.kid: Hang the forcemeter up. Hang the empty bag on it. Is the pointer at zero? If not, ask a grown-up to fix it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the kilogram experiment. You get a forcemeter ready, so you can weigh bags of rice in newtons. The unit Forcemeters and newtons shows how one works.

flow.do: 1. Put the bag on the kitchen scale and pour in rice until it shows 100 grams. 2. Hang the bag on the forcemeter. 3. Wait until it stops bouncing. 4. Read the pointer with your eyes level with it.
flow.say: Wait until it's completely still. While it bounces, the spring is pulling up harder, then softer. Only when it's still does the spring pull up exactly as hard as gravity pulls down.
flow.kid: Pour 100 grams of rice into the bag. Hang it up. Wait until it is still. Read the number. Write it down.

ask.q: Why do we wait until the bag is still?
good: When it's bouncing the number keeps changing.
Only when it's still does the spring pull up as hard as gravity pulls down.

flow.parent: No kitchen scale? Hang packets whose mass is printed on them instead: a 100 gram soap, a 500 gram packet of dal, a 1 kilogram packet of atta. Put each one in the bag.

flow.do: 1. Make the bag 200 grams, then 300, then 500, then 1,000 grams. 2. Each time, write your guess first. 3. Then hang it, wait, read and write.
flow.say: Before each one, guess the number. Is there a pattern?
flow.kid: Make the bag heavier: 200, 300, 500, then 1,000 grams. Guess first each time. Then weigh it. Do you see a pattern?
flow.parent: Expect about 1 newton for every 100 grams. A whole kilogram reads close to 10 newtons. A more exact value on Earth is 9.8 newtons, so a careful reading might show a little under 10. Cheap forcemeters may be out by a little. That is fine.

check.q: 100 grams of rice reads about 1 newton. About what will 500 grams read?
check.why: Every 100 grams adds about 1 newton. 500 grams is 5 lots of 100 grams, so it weighs about 5 newtons. Picking 500 newtons usually means grams and newtons are being read as the same unit. They measure different things: grams measure mass, newtons measure force. Picking 1 newton usually means thinking the pull stays the same however much rice there is.

flow.do: Help your child draw a line graph. Put grams along the bottom and newtons up the side. Mark a dot for each bag, then join the dots.
flow.say: Let's draw it. What shape do the dots make?
flow.kid: Draw a dot for each bag. Grams go along the bottom. Newtons go up the side. Join the dots. What shape is it?

chart.title: Made-up example: the weight of bags of rice on a forcemeter
chart.note: Each extra 100 grams adds about 1 newton. A whole kilogram, 1,000 grams, weighs about 10 newtons.

flow.think: The dots make a straight line. If you had 2 kilograms of rice, where would its dot be?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: every 100 grams of rice weighs about 1 newton, so a kilogram weighs about 10 newtons. What I saw: 100 grams read 1 newton, 500 grams read 5 newtons, and 1,000 grams read nearly 10 newtons. Why: the more rice there is, the more matter there is for the Earth to pull on, so the pull gets bigger by the same amount each time.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: the weight of bags of rice on a forcemeter
example_chart.note: Each extra 100 grams adds about 1 newton. A whole kilogram, 1,000 grams, weighs about 10 newtons.

experiments.title: The stone that gets lighter in water
experiments.question: What happens to a stone's reading on a forcemeter when we lower it into water?
experiments.predict: Guess first. When the stone goes into the water, will the reading go up, go down, or stay the same? What will happen if it rests on the bottom? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same stone, the same string and the same forcemeter every time. Hold the forcemeter still. Wait until the stone stops swinging before you read. Change only how much of the stone is in the water.
results_table: My guess: more, less or same?

materials.item: a forcemeter that measures up to 10 newtons
a stone about the size of a big lemon, from a plant pot or the building compound, tied tightly with string (or a big potato, if you have no stone)
a bucket or a big steel vessel of water
a towel for spills

experiments.safety: Do this outside or in the bathroom. Wipe up spilled water so nobody slips.

schedule.what: Weigh the stone in air, half in water, fully in water, and resting on the bottom.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar for each reading. Draw an arrow on the stone for each push or pull on it.
experiments.context: In this experiment you hang a stone from a forcemeter and lower it into a bucket of water. You find out how water pushes up on things.

flow.do: 1. Tie the string tightly round the stone, with a loop at the top. 2. Hang the loop on the forcemeter. 3. Hold the forcemeter still, with the stone in the air. 4. Read and write the number.
flow.say: First, how much does the stone weigh in the air? That's how hard the Earth pulls it.
flow.kid: Tie the stone on its string. Hang it from the forcemeter. Hold it still in the air. Read the number. Write it down.
flow.context: This is the first step of the stone in water experiment. You weigh a stone in the air before you lower it into water.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to guess what will happen in the water. 2. Lower the stone until half of it is under the water. Read it. 3. Lower it until all of it is under, but not touching the bottom. Read it.
flow.say: Did any of the stone come off? Did the Earth stop pulling it? So why did the number go down?
flow.kid: Guess first! Lower the stone halfway into the water. Read the number. Now put it all the way under. Don't touch the bottom. Read again.

check.q: The stone read 3 newtons in the air and 2 newtons under the water. Why?
options: The water pushes up on the stone, so the spring holds less
The stone got smaller in the water
check.why: The water pushes up on the stone. That push is called upthrust. Now the spring and the water share the job of holding the stone, so the spring holds less. The Earth still pulls the stone just as hard. Picking 'gravity is weaker under water' is a very common idea, because things feel light in water. But the lightness comes from the water's push.

flow.parent: A potato works too, and gives an even bigger drop. That is because a potato is only a little heavier than the same amount of water.

flow.do: 1. Lower the stone until it rests on the bottom of the bucket. 2. Read the forcemeter. 3. Lift the stone out of the water and read it again.
flow.say: Now the bottom of the bucket is helping too. What does the forcemeter say? And when we lift it out?
flow.kid: Let the stone rest on the bottom. Read the number. Now lift it right out. Is it back to the first number?
flow.parent: On the bottom, the string goes slack and the reading drops to zero, because the bucket's floor is holding the stone up. Out of the water, it goes back to the air reading. Nothing about the stone changed. Only the things holding it up changed.

chart.title: Made-up example: a stone on a forcemeter, in air and in water
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what results can look like. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: Talk about swimming pools and floating. If you can, feel it yourself. Lift a full mug of water while it is under the water in a bucket. Then lift it out into the air.
flow.say: When you float in a pool, the water does the same thing to you. The Earth still pulls you. The water pushes up on every part of you that is under it.
flow.kid: In a pool, water pushes up on you too. The Earth still pulls you just as hard. The water holds you up. That is why you feel light.
flow.think: In a pool, why might lifting your arms out of the water make you sink a little?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: water pushes up on things in it, so they seem lighter, but gravity does not change. What I saw: the stone read 3 newtons in the air, 2 newtons under the water, and 3 newtons again when I lifted it out. Why: the water helped hold the stone up, so the forcemeter's spring had less to hold.

experiments.title: A forcemeter in a lift
experiments.question: Does a bag's reading on a forcemeter change while a lift goes up and down?
experiments.predict: Guess first. When the lift starts to go up, will the reading go up, go down, or stay the same? What about when it slows down at the top? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same bag and the same forcemeter. Hold your arm still, close to your body, so only the lift moves the bag. Watch the reading at four moments: starting, moving steadily, slowing and stopped. If you have no lift, move the forcemeter up and down with your arm instead, quickly and then slowly.
results_table: My guess: more, less or same?

materials.item: a forcemeter that measures up to 20 newtons
a 1 litre bottle of water in a cloth bag, which is about 1 kilogram
a lift in a block of flats, an office, a mall or a hospital
a phone to film the pointer, if you have one

experiments.safety: A grown-up comes in the lift. Choose a quiet time, and do not get in anyone's way. Stand still, and keep the bag away from the doors.

schedule.what: Ride a lift up and down with a bag hanging from a forcemeter. Watch the reading at each moment.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a line graph of the reading during the ride, or watch the film and write the numbers.
experiments.context: In this experiment you take a forcemeter with a bag hanging from it into a lift. You watch the reading change as the lift starts, moves and stops.

flow.do: 1. Hang the bag from the forcemeter. 2. Read it while you stand still on the ground floor. 3. Write it down.
flow.say: First, what does the bag read when everything is still? That's our starting number.
flow.kid: Hang the bag on the forcemeter. Stand still. Read the number. Write it down. Now guess: what happens when the lift moves?
flow.context: This is the first step of the lift experiment. You weigh a bag on a forcemeter while standing still, before taking it on a lift ride.

flow.do: 1. Get in the lift and press a button for a floor high up. 2. Hold the forcemeter still. 3. Watch the pointer as the lift starts, while it moves, and as it slows and stops. 4. Film it if you can.
flow.say: Watch closely. The lift is starting. What is the pointer doing? Now we're moving steadily. And now we're slowing down.
flow.kid: Watch the pointer! The lift starts. Up or down? Now it moves steadily. Now it slows. What happens each time?
flow.parent: Going up, the reading rises a little as the lift starts. It goes back to normal while the lift moves steadily. It dips a little as the lift slows at the top. Coming down, it is the other way round. The changes are small, often about half a newton to 1 newton. Filming helps.

chart.title: Made-up example: a 1 kilogram bag on a forcemeter during a lift ride up
chart.note: Standing still: 10 newtons. The lift starts up: 11. Going up steadily: 10. Slowing down at the top: 9. Stopped: 10.

flow.do: Ride down again and watch the same four moments. If you have no lift, do this at home: move the forcemeter up quickly, then stop it, then move it down quickly.
flow.say: Going down, what happens at the start? Did your own legs feel the same thing?
flow.kid: Ride down. Watch the pointer again. Did your legs feel heavy or floaty? At the same moments as the bag?

check.q: A lift starts to go up. The bag's reading goes from 10 newtons to 11 newtons. What happened?
options: The spring had to pull harder to speed the bag up
More water got into the bottle
check.why: To start the bag moving upwards, the spring must pull it up harder than gravity pulls it down. So the reading goes up for a moment. Gravity is just the same. The bottle has the same water in it. Picking 'gravity got stronger' is a natural guess, because you feel heavier too. But your heavy feeling is the floor pushing harder on you.

flow.do: Talk about other places you feel heavy or light. Think of a swing, a giant wheel at a mela, or a bus going over a bump.
flow.say: Where else have you felt heavy for a moment, or floaty? What was speeding up or slowing down?
flow.kid: Where else do you feel heavy, or floaty? On a swing? On a giant wheel? Was something speeding up or slowing down?
flow.think: At the very top of a swing, you feel floaty. Has gravity let go of you, or has something else changed?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a forcemeter reads more when a lift starts going up, and less when it slows at the top, but gravity stays the same. What I saw: the bag read 10 newtons standing still and 11 as the lift started up. It read 10 while moving steadily, and 9 as it slowed at the top. Why: to speed the bag up, the spring had to pull harder. To slow it down, the spring pulled less.

example_chart.note: Standing still: 10 newtons. The lift starts up: 11. Going up steadily: 10. Slowing down at the top: 9. Stopped: 10.
