experiments.title: Drop it! Where does weight go when things fall?
experiments.question: Does a falling thing still press on what is holding it?
experiments.predict: Guess first. If we drop a leaking bottle of water, will the water keep squirting out while it falls? If we drop coins hanging on a rubber band, will the band stay stretched? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Drop each thing from the same height, about as high as a grown-up's head, onto the same soft landing place. Watch, or film it in slow motion. Do each drop three times, because each fall is very quick.

materials.item: an empty plastic water bottle with two small holes near the bottom, made by a grown-up with a drawing pin or a thick needle
a clear plastic bottle with its cap, a short thin rubber band, and about ten coins taped into a small stack
a bucket, and a pillow or a bed to land on
a phone that can film in slow motion, if you have one

experiments.safety: A grown-up makes the holes. Do the water drop in the bathroom over a bucket, or outside. Drop things only into the bucket or onto a pillow or bed, never near anyone's feet.

schedule.what: Drop a leaking bottle, and a bottle with coins on a rubber band, and watch what happens while they fall.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the bottle before the drop and during the fall.
experiments.context: In this experiment you drop a leaking bottle of water, and a bottle with coins hanging inside it on a rubber band. You find out what happens to weight while something falls.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up pokes two small holes near the bottom of an empty bottle. 2. Take the cap off, so air can get in. 3. Cover the holes with your fingers and fill the bottle with water. 4. In the bathroom, hold it high over a bucket and uncover the holes. Watch the water squirt out.
flow.say: Look at the water squirting out. Why do you think it squirts? Now guess. If I drop the bottle, will the water keep squirting? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Fill the leaky bottle. Hold it up high. Watch the water squirt out. Now guess. Will it still squirt while it falls?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Drop It experiment. You make a leaking bottle of water, to see what happens to it while it falls.

flow.do: 1. Hold the squirting bottle high over the bucket. 2. Let go. 3. Watch the holes closely while it falls. 4. Film it in slow motion if you can. Do it three times.
flow.say: Watch the holes, not the bottle. What happens to the squirting while it falls?
flow.kid: Let go of the bottle! Watch the holes as it falls. Does the water still squirt out? Try three times.

check.q: While the leaking bottle falls, the squirting stops. Why?
options: The water and the bottle fall together, so the water stops pressing on the bottle
check.why: While it falls, the water and the bottle fall together at the same speed. The water no longer presses down on the bottom of the bottle, so it stops squeezing out of the holes. Gravity is still pulling both of them. That is why they are falling! Picking 'gravity stops' is a natural guess. But a falling thing is falling because gravity pulls it.

flow.parent: The cap must be off, or air cannot get in and the water only dribbles. Let go cleanly, without throwing or spinning the bottle. The fall lasts less than a second, so watch the holes, not the bottle. A slow-motion film shows it best.

flow.do: 1. Tape the stack of coins to one end of the rubber band. 2. Lower the coins into the bottle, and hang the other end of the band over the rim of the bottle's mouth. 3. Screw the cap on over the band, so the cap holds it tight. The coins should hang clear of the bottom, stretching the band. 4. Hold the bottle upright above a pillow and look at the band. 5. Drop the bottle onto the pillow, watching the band. Do it three times.
flow.say: The coins stretch the band, like a tiny forcemeter. What will the band do while the bottle falls?
flow.kid: The coins stretch the rubber band, like a forcemeter. Drop the bottle onto a pillow. Watch the band. Does it stay stretched?
flow.parent: If the coins touch the bottom, use fewer coins or a shorter band. While it falls, the band springs back and pulls the coins up towards the cap. The coins no longer pull down on the band, because they are falling just as fast as the bottle. A forcemeter dropped onto a bed does the same: its pointer jumps back to zero.

flow.do: Talk about astronauts in the space station.
flow.say: Astronauts in the space station are like the water in our falling bottle. They and the station are falling together, all the time. So nothing presses on anything. That's why they float.
flow.kid: Astronauts are like the water in the falling bottle. They and their station fall together. Nothing presses on anything. So they float!
flow.think: If you stood on a bathroom scale and both of you fell together, what would the scale show?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: falling things stop pressing on what holds them, so they feel weightless, but gravity still pulls them. What I saw: the water stopped squirting while the bottle fell. The rubber band sprang back and pulled the coins up while the bottle fell onto the pillow. Why: everything was falling together at the same speed, so nothing had to hold anything else up.

activities.title: Who Is Holding You Up?

materials.item: a wall, a cushion, a bucket of water, and a soft mattress or carpet

activities.safety: In the falling game, the faller leans back only a hand's width, and the catcher is a grown-up standing close behind.

schedule.what: Press on different things, catch a falling friend, and find everything that holds you up.

activities.record: Draw yourself standing, sitting and lying down. Draw an arrow for gravity's pull and an arrow for each push holding you up.
activities.context: This is a hands-on activity about the support force: the push from floors, chairs, water and hands that holds us up against gravity.

flow.do: 1. Your child presses a hand flat on a wall. 2. Then into a cushion. 3. Then into a bucket of water.
flow.say: Which one stopped your hand? Which one let your hand in? Each one pushes back, but some push back harder.
flow.kid: Press your hand on a wall. Now into a cushion. Now into water. Which one pushes back hardest?

ask.q: Why can't your hand go into the wall?
good: The electrons of the wall repel the electrons of my hand.

flow.context: This is the first step of Who Is Holding You Up? You press on hard and soft things to feel how they push back. That push is called the support force.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up stands right behind the child on a soft floor. 2. The child stands stiff like a plank, arms crossed. 3. The child leans back a hand's width into the grown-up's hands. 4. The grown-up pushes them back up. Do not swap. A child must never try to catch a grown-up.
flow.say: When I caught you, my hands were doing the floor's job. Gravity was still pulling you, but my hands pushed back, so you did not fall.
flow.kid: Stand stiff like a plank. Lean back a tiny bit. A grown-up catches you. Their hands hold you up, like the floor does.

check.q: When a grown-up catches you as you lean back, what stops you falling?
options: Their hands push up on you, against gravity
check.why: The catcher's hands push on you and stop you falling. That push is a support force, like the floor's. Gravity never switches off. Picking 'the air holds you up' usually means thinking air is strong. Air pushes back only a little, which is why we fall through it.

flow.do: Go round the home and find everything holding someone or something up. Look at the floor, chairs, beds, shelves, hooks and buckets of water.
flow.say: Gravity is pulling everything in this house down. Let's find what is holding each thing up.
flow.kid: Gravity pulls everything down. Find 10 things holding something up. A shelf holds books. What else?
flow.parent: Good finds: the bed holds you at night, a shelf holds books and a hook holds a bag. A table holds plates. The water in a bucket holds up a floating cup. Even the walls hold up the roof.

flow.do: Lie down flat on the floor together, and feel where the floor pushes on you.
flow.say: Lie still. Feel the floor pushing up on your back, your head and your heels. It has been doing that all day, every day.
flow.kid: Lie flat on the floor. Feel where the floor pushes on you. It holds you up all day!
flow.think: Gravity pulls on every part of you. But the floor pushes only where you touch it. Lying down, it pushes on much more of you. Is that why lying down feels so restful?

activities.title: Two Scales, One You

materials.item: two bathroom scales, or one bathroom scale and a pile of books the same height
a heavy bag, like a school bag full of books

activities.safety: Put the scales on a hard, flat floor. Stand on them slowly, and hold a grown-up's hand when you lean or stand on one leg.

schedule.what: Stand with one foot on each scale. Lean, lift a leg and hold a bag, and watch the numbers.

activities.record: Write the two numbers for each test, and add them up. Does the total change?
activities.context: In this activity you stand with one foot on each of two bathroom scales. You lean, lift a leg and hold a heavy bag, and watch how the two scales share your weight.

flow.do: 1. Put two scales side by side. 2. Your child stands with one foot on each. 3. Read both numbers and add them up.
flow.say: Each scale is holding up part of you. Let's add them. That's the push holding all of you up.
flow.kid: Put one foot on each scale. Read both numbers. Add them up. That is all of you!
flow.parent: Bathroom scales show kilograms, not newtons. They measure how hard you press, then work out the kilograms for the Earth's pull. A dial scale shows changes as they happen. A digital scale may freeze its first number, so step off and on again for each reading. If you only have one scale, put a pile of books of the same height beside it, and read just the one scale.
flow.context: This is the first step of Two Scales, One You. You stand with one foot on each of two bathroom scales, to see how they share your weight.

flow.do: 1. Your child leans slowly to the left, then to the right. 2. Then lifts one foot off one scale, holding your hand. 3. Write both numbers each time, and the total.
flow.say: Lean to one side. What happens to the numbers? And the total?
flow.kid: Lean to one side. Watch both numbers. Now lift one foot. Add up the numbers each time. Does the total change?

check.q: You stand on two scales. They read 15 kilograms and 15 kilograms. You lean left, and the left one reads 20 kilograms. What does the right one read?
check.why: You have not changed, so the total stays 30 kilograms. If the left scale shows 20, the right one shows the rest: 30 take away 20 is 10. Picking 15 usually means thinking each scale measures only its own foot, whatever you do. Picking 20 usually means thinking leaning adds weight. Leaning just moves your weight from one foot to the other.

flow.do: 1. Your child holds the heavy bag while standing on both scales. 2. Read both numbers and the total.
flow.say: Now the scales are holding you and the bag. What happened to the total?
flow.kid: Hold the heavy bag. Read both numbers. Add them up. What changed?

flow.do: Try tree pose on one scale: stand on one leg, with the other foot resting on your knee.
flow.say: In tree pose, one foot holds up all of you. Can you feel your weight move as you wobble?
flow.kid: Do tree pose on one scale. Watch the number as you wobble. Does it jump about?
flow.think: When you wobble, the number jumps. When you are perfectly still, it settles. Why?

activities.title: The Space Marathon (act it out)

materials.item: a long dupatta or a towel
a pillow and some open space

activities.safety: Press down gently, never hard. Do the floating part on a soft mattress or carpet.

schedule.what: Act out astronauts floating, and Sunita Williams running a marathon in space.

activities.record: Draw an astronaut running on a treadmill in space, with the stretchy cords pulling her down.
activities.context: This is a short play about life in the International Space Station, where astronauts float because they are falling all the time. It includes Sunita Williams, who ran a marathon in space in 2007.

flow.do: Your child pretends to float through the space station. They move slowly, push gently off walls, and pretend to catch a floating ball of water in their mouth.
flow.say: In the space station, nothing pushes on you, because you and the station are falling together. So you float. Show me how you'd move.
flow.kid: You are an astronaut! You float. Move slowly. Push gently off the wall. Catch a floating ball of water with your mouth!
flow.context: This is the first step of the Space Marathon play. You pretend to float in the space station, where astronauts feel weightless.

flow.do: 1. Tell the true story of Sunita Williams. 2. Your child jogs on the spot. 3. A grown-up loops a dupatta over the child's shoulders, holds both ends low and pulls down very gently.
flow.say: In 2007, Sunita Williams ran the Boston Marathon in the space station, on a treadmill. But floating feet can't push on a treadmill. So stretchy cords pulled her down onto it. I'm being your stretchy cords.
flow.kid: Sunita Williams ran a marathon in space! Stretchy cords pulled her down. Jog on the spot. A grown-up gently pulls you down with a dupatta.

check.q: Why did Sunita Williams need stretchy cords to run on a treadmill in space?
options: Without them she would float off, and her feet could not push on the treadmill
Gravity in space is too strong
To stop the treadmill floating away
check.why: In the space station, nothing presses her feet onto the floor, because she and the station fall together. Without a push between her feet and the treadmill, she couldn't run. The cords pulled her down so her feet pressed on it, like weight does on Earth. Picking 'gravity is too strong' mixes things up. Gravity is there, but she feels no weight, because she is falling.

flow.do: Talk about why astronauts exercise for about two hours every day.
flow.say: On Earth, your bones carry your weight every day, and that keeps them strong. In space, bones carry no weight, so they get weaker. That's why astronauts exercise every day.
flow.kid: Your bones carry your weight all day. That keeps them strong. In space, bones get weaker. So astronauts exercise every day. Jump ten times now!
flow.think: Your bones grow strong because they carry your weight. What else grows stronger when it carries something heavy?

activities.title: Heavy Words: guru, laghu and gravitas

materials.item: paper, a pencil, and a short poem or song you know

schedule.what: Find words that come from 'heavy', and clap heavy and light beats.

activities.record: Make a word tree. Write 'heavy' at the bottom, and the words that grew from it on the branches.
activities.context: This activity is about words. In Sanskrit, 'guru' means heavy and 'laghu' means light. In Latin, 'gravis' means heavy. Many words we use today grew from them, including gravity.

flow.do: Tell your child where these words come from. Write them on paper as a word tree.
flow.say: In Sanskrit, guru means heavy. A guru is a teacher whose words have weight. Gurutva means heaviness, and gurutvakarshan means gravity, the pull of heaviness. In Latin, gravis means heavy. It gave English the words gravity, gravitas, and grave, which means serious.
flow.kid: Guru means heavy in Sanskrit. A guru is a teacher whose words are 'heavy'. Gravity comes from gravis, which means heavy in Latin.
flow.context: This is the first step of Heavy Words. You find out how the words guru, gravity and gravitas all come from old words meaning heavy.

flow.do: 1. Clap a name or a short line of a poem. 2. Long, heavy syllables get a big clap. Short, light ones get a small tap.
flow.say: Old Indian poets called long syllables guru, heavy, and short ones laghu, light. Let's clap them. Big clap for heavy, small tap for light.
flow.kid: Clap your name. Long sounds are heavy, guru: big clap! Short sounds are light, laghu: small tap!

check.q: In Sanskrit, what does the word guru mean?
check.why: Guru means heavy, and laghu means light. A guru, a teacher, is someone whose words carry weight. The word for gravity in Hindi and many Indian languages, gurutvakarshan, means the pull of heaviness. Picking 'bright' is a lovely guess, because a good teacher brings light. But the word really means heavy.

flow.do: Talk about what gravitas means in a person.
flow.say: People say a calm, serious person who makes others listen has gravitas, weight. Who do you know who has gravitas? Can a child have it?
flow.kid: A calm person who makes others listen has gravitas. Who has it in your family? Can you have it too?
flow.think: Is being 'heavy' a good thing? When is it good to be light?

activities.title: A Day of Heavy and Light: the feel-weight hunt

materials.item: a small notebook and a pencil, to carry for a day

activities.safety: Notice feelings only during ordinary things. Don't jump off high places to test it.

schedule.what: Get the notebook ready. Carry it all day, and write down each heavy or light moment.
Read the notebook together. For each moment, work out what was pushing harder or less.

activities.record: A list of moments, each marked HEAVY or LIGHT, with what was speeding up, slowing down or holding you.
activities.context: This is a two-day hunt for moments when you feel heavier or lighter than usual. Think of a swing, a lift or a pool. Then you work out why.

flow.do: Draw two columns in the notebook: HEAVY and LIGHT. Give it to your child to carry all day.
flow.say: Today you're a weight detective. Every time you feel heavier or lighter than usual, write it down.
flow.kid: You are a weight detective today. Feel heavy? Write it under HEAVY. Feel floaty? Write it under LIGHT.
flow.context: This is the first step of the feel-weight hunt. All day you notice moments when you feel heavier or lighter than usual.

flow.do: On the next day, read the list together. For each moment, ask what was holding your child, and whether it was pushing harder or less.
flow.wait: Carry the notebook for one whole day first.
flow.say: Let's look at your list. At each moment, did gravity change? Or did the push holding you up change?
flow.kid: Read your list. Did gravity change? Or did the push holding you change? Was something speeding up or slowing down?
flow.parent: Good finds: the bottom of a swing feels heavy, the top feels light. Lying in a pool feels light because the water pushes up. A bus going over a bump feels heavy, then light. Jumping off a step feels light for a moment. In every case, gravity stays the same.

check.q: At the top of a swing you feel floaty. Why?
options: The seat is pushing up on you less
Gravity has let go of you
check.why: At the top, you are starting to fall back, so the seat pushes up on you less. You feel lighter because the push is smaller. Gravity pulls you just as hard at the top as at the bottom. Picking 'gravity has let go' is how it feels. But gravity never lets go.

projects.title: The Root That Knows Which Way Is Down

materials.item: a clear glass jar or plastic cup
kitchen paper or cotton wool, and water
4 to 6 seeds that sprout fast, like moong or chana, soaked overnight
a marker pen and a notebook

projects.safety: Wash your hands after touching the seeds. Don't eat seeds that have been used in the experiment.

schedule.what: Soak the seeds. Line the jar with wet paper. Push the seeds between the paper and the glass.
Look for tiny roots. Draw them. Keep the paper wet.
When the roots are about 2 cm long, lay the jar on its side. Mark the direction each root points.
Look again. Have the roots bent? Draw them.
Compare all your drawings. Talk about how a root knows which way is down.

projects.record: Draw the roots every day. Use an arrow to show which way is down. Write the day under each drawing.
projects.context: In this 6-day project you grow moong or chana seeds in a jar, then lay the jar on its side. You watch the roots bend to grow downwards again, and find out how plants feel which way is down.

flow.do: 1. Soak 6 moong or chana seeds in water overnight. 2. Line the inside of a clear jar with wet kitchen paper. 3. Push the seeds between the paper and the glass, so you can see them. 4. Put a little water in the bottom.
flow.say: Plants have no eyes. But they always know which way is down. Let's find out how good they are at it.
flow.kid: Line a jar with wet paper. Push the soaked seeds between the paper and the glass. Keep the paper wet.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Root That Knows Which Way Is Down. You grow seeds in a clear jar, so you can watch their roots.

flow.do: Look at the seeds each day. Draw the tiny roots when they appear. Keep the paper wet.
flow.wait: Wait 1 to 2 days, until the roots are about 2 cm long.
flow.say: Which way are the roots growing?
flow.kid: Look at your seeds every day. When you see tiny roots, draw them. Which way do they grow?

flow.do: 1. When the roots are about 2 cm long, lay the jar gently on its side. 2. With the marker, draw a small arrow on the glass beside each root tip, showing which way it points now.
flow.say: Now the roots are pointing sideways. Down is a different way for them now. Will they notice?
flow.kid: Lay the jar on its side. The roots now point sideways. Mark each root tip on the glass. Will they turn?

flow.do: Look at the roots each day for three days. Draw them each time.
flow.wait: Check once a day for 3 days.
flow.say: Have the roots turned? Which way?
flow.kid: Look every day. Have the roots bent? Which way are they growing now? Draw them.

check.q: You laid the jar on its side. After a day or two, which way do the roots grow?
options: They bend to grow downwards again
They turn upwards towards the light
check.why: Roots bend to grow downwards, towards the pull of gravity. Scientists call this gravitropism. Most think tiny heavy grains of starch inside root-tip cells sink to the bottom, like sand in water. The cells feel where the grains settle. Picking 'towards the light' mixes roots with shoots. Shoots usually grow up towards light. Roots grow down.

flow.do: Put all the drawings side by side. Explain how scientists think a root feels gravity.
flow.say: Inside the root tip are cells holding tiny heavy grains of starch. The grains sink to the bottom of each cell. The cell feels where they land. So each cell knows which way is down.
flow.kid: Root tip cells have tiny heavy grains inside. The grains sink to the bottom of each cell. So the cell knows which way is down!
flow.think: Astronauts have grown plants in the space station, where everything floats. Which way do you think the roots grew?
flow.parent: In the space station, roots tend to grow away from the seed, and towards water and sometimes light. Without felt weight, the starch grains don't settle. Scientists are still studying exactly how plants sense gravity.

challenges.title: Weigh It in Space
challenges.problem: In the space station, everything floats. A forcemeter or a scale reads zero, because nothing presses on it. But doctors still need to know each astronaut's mass. Find a way to compare masses that would still work with no weight.
constraints: Your method must not use the weight of the thing.
You can only use things from home.
Test it here on Earth, but explain why it would also work in space.
materials: a few things to compare, like an eraser, a ₹5 coin, a small stone and a bunch of keys
general: Push each thing with the same small push, and see how fast it moves. A bigger mass speeds up less.
Tape the thing to the end of a ruler held over a table edge. Twang the ruler and watch. A bigger mass makes it wobble more slowly.
Astronauts really do this. Since the 1970s, they have sat in a special chair on a spring and rocked back and forth. A computer times the rocking to find each person's mass.
creative: Tie each thing to a rubber band and whirl it round at the same speed. A bigger mass stretches the band more.
Roll each thing at the same speed into a paper cup and see how far the cup moves.
Use a stretchy rubber band to catapult each thing gently along the floor. Lighter things fly further.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way to compare masses without weight. Draw it, test it on three things, and explain why it would work in the space station.
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. In the space station, nothing has weight you can feel, so scales do not work. You must find another way to compare masses.

flow.do: Explain the problem. Hold up a forcemeter and remind your child what it reads when it falls.
flow.say: In the space station, a forcemeter reads zero for everything. But an astronaut still has mass. How could a doctor find it?
flow.kid: In space, a forcemeter reads zero for everything. But things still have mass. How can we compare them?
flow.context: This is the first step of Weigh It in Space. You must find a way to compare masses that would work even where nothing has weight you can feel.

flow.do: List three ideas together before trying anything.
flow.say: Mass makes things hard to push and hard to start moving. Can we use that?
flow.kid: Think like an engineer. Draw three ideas first. Mass makes things hard to push. Can you use that?

flow.do: 1. Hold a ruler flat on the table with about 20 cm sticking out over the edge. Press the other end down hard. 2. Tape the eraser to the free end. 3. Twang it and watch how fast it wobbles. Film it in slow motion if you can, and count the wobbles in the first 2 seconds. 4. Do the same with the coin, the stone and the keys.
flow.say: Twang the ruler. Does it wobble fast or slow? Which thing makes the ruler wobble slowest?
flow.kid: Tape a thing to the end of the ruler. Twang it! Does it wobble fast or slow? Try each thing.

check.q: In a slow-motion film, the ruler with keys wobbles 5 times in 2 seconds. With an eraser, it wobbles 10 times. Which has more mass?
options: We can't tell without a scale
check.why: A bigger mass is harder to swing back and forth, so it wobbles more slowly. The keys made fewer wobbles, so they have more mass. This works in space too, because it uses mass, not weight. Picking 'the eraser' usually means more wobbles was read as more mass. Here, slower wobbles mean more mass.

flow.parent: Hold the ruler down firmly with your hand so only the end moves. The wobbles die away in a few seconds, so watch the first moment closely. Filming in slow motion makes counting much easier.

flow.do: Read the usual solutions and the creative ideas together. Then invent a new one.
flow.say: Astronauts really sit on a chair on a spring and rock back and forth. A computer times the rocking. That's our ruler idea, but for a whole person!
flow.kid: Astronauts really rock on a spring chair to find their mass. Like your ruler! Can you invent a new way?
flow.think: Mass makes things heavy and hard to push. Why do you think those two always go together?

challenges.title: The Coin Raft
challenges.problem: Build a raft from one sheet of aluminium foil that floats in a bucket of water while holding as many coins as possible.
constraints: Use only one sheet of foil, about as big as a page of a notebook.
The raft must float for 10 seconds without sinking.
materials: a sheet of aluminium foil, about 20 cm by 30 cm
a bucket or a big vessel of water
the coins you have at home, all of one kind if you can, or dry chana added one spoonful at a time
general: Fold up the edges to make a wide, flat boat with low walls.
Spread the coins out evenly, so one side does not tip.
A wider boat pushes more water aside, so the water can push up harder.
creative: Copy the shape of the giant makhana leaf: very wide and flat, with a little rim.
Make a second raft with slightly higher walls, and see if it holds more coins.
Add coins in rings from the middle outwards.
challenges.your_turn: Design your own raft. Count your coins. Then change one thing about your design and try to beat your own record.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about how water holds up weight. You build a foil raft and see how many coins it can carry before it sinks.

flow.do: 1. Squeeze a small piece of foil into the tightest ball you can. A grown-up can press it harder with the base of a steel tumbler. Drop it in the water. 2. Then lay a flat piece of the same size on the water.
flow.say: Same foil, same mass. Why does the ball sink while the flat one floats?
flow.kid: Crumple a bit of foil into a ball. Drop it in. Now lay a flat piece on the water. Which floats?
flow.context: This is the first step of The Coin Raft. You compare a crumpled ball of foil with a flat sheet, to see how shape helps water hold things up.
flow.parent: A loose ball traps air inside and may float. Squeezed really tight, it sinks.

flow.do: Think about the shape before building.
flow.say: The water pushes up on whatever pushes it aside. How could your raft push lots of water aside?
flow.kid: Draw your raft first. How can you make it push lots of water aside?

check.q: Why does a flat, wide foil boat hold more coins than a crumpled ball of foil?
options: It pushes more water aside, so the water pushes up on it harder
The flat foil has less weight
Flat things are not pulled by gravity
check.why: Both have the same mass and the same weight. But the wide boat pushes a lot of water aside as it sits low in the water. The more water a thing pushes aside, the harder the water pushes up on it. Picking 'flat foil has less weight' is a common guess. Shape does not change weight. It changes how much the water can help.

flow.do: 1. Build the raft. 2. Float it. 3. Add coins one at a time, spread out. 4. Count until it sinks. 5. Change the design and try again.
flow.say: Add the coins one at a time. Count out loud. How many before it sinks?
flow.kid: Float your raft. Add coins one at a time. Count! How many before it sinks? Then try a better design.
flow.parent: Good rafts with low, wide walls can hold more than 100 coins, so you may run out. If you do, add spoonfuls of dry chana instead, and count the spoons. The raft sinks when water spills over the edge, or when one side dips.

flow.do: Compare designs, and look at the usual and creative solutions together.
flow.say: Ships are made of heavy steel, yet they float. Can you explain why now?
flow.kid: Big ships are made of steel. Steel sinks! So why do ships float? Use your raft to explain.
flow.think: The water never takes away the coins' weight. It only holds it. How much can water hold?

items.p: What is weight?
opts: How much matter a thing has
The pull of gravity on a thing
items.why: Weight is the pull of gravity on a thing. Picking 'how much matter' mixes up weight with mass. Mass is the amount of matter, and weight is the pull on it. Picking 'how big' is a common idea, but a big cushion can weigh less than a small stone.

items.p: What do scientists measure weight in?
items.why: Weight is a force, and forces are measured in newtons. Picking kilograms is very common, because shops use kilograms. Kilograms measure mass, the amount of matter.

items.p: How much matter a thing has is called its ____.
items.why: Mass is how much matter a thing has. It is measured in grams and kilograms.

items.p: On Earth, about how much does a 1 kilogram bag of rice weigh on a forcemeter?
items.why: Every 100 grams weighs about 1 newton. 1 kilogram is 1,000 grams, so it weighs about 10 newtons. Picking 1,000 newtons usually means grams were counted as newtons. Picking 1 newton usually means thinking 1 kilogram and 1 newton are the same.
items.context: A forcemeter is a spring tool that measures weight in newtons. You hang a thing on its hook and read the pointer.

items.p: Why must you wait until the bag stops bouncing before you read a forcemeter?
opts: Only when it is still does the spring pull up exactly as hard as gravity pulls down
The numbers only appear when it is still
items.why: While the bag bounces, the spring pulls sometimes harder and sometimes softer than gravity. When it is still, the two pulls are equal, so the reading shows the weight. Picking 'bouncing makes the bag heavier' is close: the reading does jump up, but the bag's weight has not changed.
items.context: A forcemeter is a spring tool that measures weight in newtons. You hang a thing on its hook and read the pointer.

items.p: Your mass is the same on the Moon as on the Earth.
items.why: True. You are made of the same matter wherever you go. Only your weight changes, because the Moon pulls more weakly.

items.p: Your weight is the same on the Moon as on the Earth.
items.why: False. The Moon pulls about one sixth as hard as the Earth, so you weigh about one sixth as much there.

items.p: You are standing on the floor. Why don't you sink into it?
opts: The floor pushes up on you as hard as you press down
Gravity does not pull you indoors
The air under you holds you up
items.why: The floor pushes back up on you. This push is called the support force. It comes from the floor's atoms pushing your atoms away. Picking 'gravity does not pull you indoors' usually means thinking roofs block gravity. Nothing blocks gravity.

items.p: A stone hangs on a forcemeter. It reads 3 newtons in the air. You lower it all the way into water. What will it read?
items.why: The water pushes up on the stone, so the spring has less to hold. The reading drops, for example to 2 newtons. Picking 'zero' usually means thinking water takes away all weight. The water holds up only part of the stone's weight. The reading drops to zero only if the stone rests on the bottom.
items.context: A forcemeter is a spring tool that measures weight in newtons. You hang a thing on its hook and read the pointer.

items.p: The push of water up on a thing in it is called ____.
items.why: Upthrust is the push of water, or air, up on things in it. It makes things feel lighter in water.

items.p: Astronauts float inside the International Space Station. Why?
opts: There is no gravity in space
They and the station are falling together, so nothing pushes on them
Their suits have balloons in them
items.why: Gravity at the space station is still about 90 out of every 100 parts as strong as on the ground. The station and everyone inside are falling round the Earth together. So nothing presses on anything, and they feel weightless. Picking 'no gravity' is the most common mix-up of all.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: the pull of gravity on a thing
how much matter a thing has
the unit for force and weight
the push of a floor or chair holding you up
items.why: Weight is a pull, measured in newtons. Mass is the amount of matter, measured in kilograms. The support force is the push that holds you up.

items.p: Sort these. Does the Earth's pull on you CHANGE, or STAY THE SAME?
items: floating in a pool
Stays the same
riding in a lift
Stays the same
jumping off a step
Stays the same
standing on the Moon
Changes a lot
sitting on a chair
Stays the same
items.why: On the Earth, gravity's pull on you hardly changes, wherever you are. What changes in a pool, a lift or a jump is the push holding you up. On the Moon, it is a different world's pull, about one sixth as strong.

items.p: You feel lighter in a swimming pool. Is gravity weaker there? Explain.
items.a: No. Gravity pulls me just as hard in the pool. The water pushes up on me, so it helps hold me up. That is why I feel lighter.
items.why: Feeling lighter comes from the water's push, called upthrust, not from less gravity.

items.p: Draw yourself standing on the floor. Draw one arrow for gravity's pull and one arrow for the floor's push.
items.a: The gravity arrow points down from the middle of the body. The floor's arrow points up from the feet. The two arrows are the same length.
items.why: When you stand still, the floor pushes up exactly as hard as gravity pulls down.
items.art: An outline of a child standing on a floor, with space for arrows.

items.p: A bag of rice hangs still from a forcemeter. Show the two forces on the bag.
items.obj: a bag of rice hanging still from a forcemeter
items.why: Gravity pulls the bag down. The forcemeter's spring pulls it up just as hard, so the bag stays still.
items.context: A forcemeter is a spring tool that measures weight in newtons. You hang a thing on its hook and read the pointer.

items.p: Look at the line graph. 300 grams of rice weighed 3 newtons. What would 700 grams weigh?
items.why: Every 100 grams adds about 1 newton. 700 grams is 7 lots of 100 grams, so it weighs about 7 newtons. Picking 4 newtons usually means adding just 1 newton to the 3, instead of 1 newton for each extra 100 grams. The pattern is 1 newton for each 100 grams.
items.context: In the kilogram experiment, you hung bags of rice of different masses on a forcemeter and drew a line graph of the readings.

chart.title: Made-up example: the weight of bags of rice on a forcemeter
chart.note: Each extra 100 grams adds about 1 newton. A whole kilogram, 1,000 grams, weighs about 10 newtons.

items.p: Look at the chart of the stone. Why did it read zero when it rested on the bottom of the bucket?
opts: The bucket's floor pushed up on it too
It had lost most of its stone
Gravity is weaker at the bottom of a bucket
items.why: On the bottom, the bucket's floor held the stone up, so the string went slack and the spring had nothing to hold. Picking 'gravity is weaker' usually means thinking the reading shows gravity directly. It shows only what the spring holds.
items.context: In the stone experiment, you hung a stone from a forcemeter and lowered it into a bucket of water. Then you let it rest on the bottom.

chart.title: Made-up example: a stone on a forcemeter, in air and in water
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what results can look like. Your numbers will be different.

items.p: The stone read 3 newtons in the air and 2 newtons under water. So the water was pushing up on it with ____ newton.
items.why: 3 take away 2 is 1. The water held up 1 newton of the stone's weight, so the spring only had to hold 2 newtons.
items.context: In the stone experiment, you hung a stone from a forcemeter and lowered it into a bucket of water.

items.p: Look at the lift graph. At which moment did the bag read the most?
opts: As the lift started going up
While the lift moved up steadily
As the lift slowed down at the top
items.why: To start the bag moving upwards, the spring had to pull harder than gravity, so the reading rose to 11 newtons. Picking 'moving up steadily' is very common. But at a steady speed, nothing is speeding up, so the reading is normal.
items.context: In the lift experiment, you hung a 1 kilogram bag from a forcemeter during a lift ride and watched the reading.

chart.title: Made-up example: a 1 kilogram bag on a forcemeter during a lift ride up
chart.note: Standing still: 10 newtons. The lift starts up: 11. Going up steadily: 10. Slowing down at the top: 9. Stopped: 10.

items.p: In a lift moving upwards at a steady speed, you feel just as heavy as when you stand still.
items.why: True. You feel heavier only while the lift speeds up. At a steady speed, the floor pushes on you just as it does when you stand still.
items.context: This question is about riding in a lift, a small room that carries people up and down a building.

items.p: A leaky bottle of water is dropped. Why does the water stop squirting while it falls?
opts: The water and bottle fall together, so the water no longer presses on the bottle
Gravity stops working on falling things
items.why: Falling together, nothing presses on anything. So the water does not squeeze out of the holes. Gravity is still pulling, which is why they fall. Picking 'gravity stops' is natural, because falling things feel weightless.
items.context: In the Drop It experiment, you made holes near the bottom of a bottle of water and dropped it while the water squirted out.

items.p: You stand with one foot on each of two bathroom scales. Both read 15 kilograms. You lift your left foot. What does the right scale read now?
items.why: Now the right scale holds up all of you, so it reads 15 + 15 = 30. Picking 15 usually means thinking each scale only ever holds one foot's share. Your weight moves to wherever you are standing.
items.context: In the Two Scales, One You activity, you stood with one foot on each of two bathroom scales.

items.p: A child has a mass of 30 kilograms. Look at the chart. About what would she weigh on the Moon?
items.why: The Moon pulls about one sixth as hard as the Earth. On Earth she weighs about 300 newtons, and 300 divided by 6 is 50. Picking '5 kilograms' mixes up mass and weight. Her mass stays 30 kilograms. Picking 1,800 means multiplying by 6 instead of dividing.
items.context: This question is about weight on other worlds. The Moon pulls about one sixth as hard as the Earth.

chart.title: The weight of a child with a mass of 30 kilograms, in different places
chart.note: The child's mass is 30 kilograms everywhere. Only the pull changes. The Sun and Jupiter have no ground to stand on, so these are 'if you could stand there' numbers.

items.p: Put these in order of how much a 30 kilogram child would weigh, from LEAST to MOST: Earth, Moon, Mars, Jupiter's cloud tops.
items: Moon
Mars
Earth
Jupiter's cloud tops
items.why: The Moon pulls weakest, about 49 newtons. Then Mars, about 111. Then the Earth, about 294. Jupiter's cloud tops pull hardest, about 744.
items.context: This question is about weight on other worlds. A child with a mass of 30 kilograms keeps that mass everywhere, but her weight changes.

items.p: How do we know the space station is not in a place with no gravity?
opts: It keeps going round the Earth instead of flying off in a straight line
It is very cold up there
items.why: Something moving with no pull on it goes in a straight line. The station keeps curving round the Earth, about 15 times a day. Only gravity can keep bending its path. Picking 'astronauts float' is the evidence many people use for no gravity. But floating happens because they are falling.

items.p: Match each place to what happens to the weight you feel.
pairs: a lift starting to go up
items.why: The weight you feel is the push holding you up. It is normal on the floor, bigger as a lift starts up, smaller in water, and zero when nothing holds you.

items.p: Gauri, in the story, sank the first time because she held her arms and head up out of the water. Explain why that made her sink.
items.a: The water can only push up on the parts of her that are in it. Her arms and head were in the air, so the water pushed on less of her. Its push was too small to hold her up.
items.why: Upthrust acts only on what is under the water. Lying back with arms spread lets the water push on all of you.
items.context: In this unit's story, Gauri is a girl in Mithila, in Bihar, who is learning to float in a pond. The first time, she panics and holds her arms and head up out of the water.

items.p: A shopkeeper says, 'This bag of sugar weighs 2 kilograms.' What would a scientist say instead, and why?
items.a: A scientist would say the bag has a mass of 2 kilograms, and a weight of about 20 newtons. Kilograms measure the amount of sugar. Newtons measure the pull of gravity on it.
items.why: Everyday talk is fine on Earth. Scientists separate mass, measured in kilograms, from weight, measured in newtons.

items.p: A child is floating still on her back in a pool. Show the forces on her.
items.obj: a child floating in a pool
items.why: Gravity pulls her down. The water pushes her up just as hard, so she floats still. There is no floor touching her.

items.p: An astronaut floats inside the space station. Show the forces on her. Careful: is anything pushing on her?
items.obj: an astronaut floating in the space station
items.why: Only gravity acts on her, pulling her towards the Earth. Nothing pushes back, which is why she feels weightless. She and the station fall together.

items.p: Draw a leaky bottle of water held still, and the same bottle falling. Show the water in each picture.
items.a: Held still: jets of water squirt out of the holes. Falling: no water comes out.
items.why: While falling, the water does not press on the bottle.
items.context: In the Drop It experiment, you dropped a bottle with holes in it while water was squirting out.

items.p: In which place would a forcemeter holding a bag read ZERO?
opts: At the bottom of a deep well
items.why: Only in free fall does the spring hold nothing at all, because the bag and forcemeter fall together. On Everest and down a well, gravity is only a tiny bit different. On the Moon, the bag still weighs about one sixth as much. Picking the Moon usually means thinking the Moon has no gravity.
items.context: A forcemeter is a spring tool that measures weight in newtons. You hang a thing on its hook and read the pointer.

items.p: You weigh slightly less at the equator than at the North Pole.
items.why: True. At the equator, you are a little further from the Earth's centre, and the Earth's spin flings you outwards a little. You weigh about half a percent less.

items.p: Light has no mass. In 1919, astronomers saw starlight bend as it passed close to the Sun. What does that tell us?
opts: Gravity works on energy, not only on mass
The Sun is made of glass
items.why: Einstein showed that energy, not only mass, is what gravity works on. Light carries energy, so gravity bends its path. Picking 'hidden mass' is a sensible guess. But light really has zero mass. Its energy is enough.
items.context: During a total eclipse of the Sun in 1919, astronomers photographed stars close to the darkened Sun.

items.p: Einstein showed that mass is a kind of energy. Which of these is an example?
opts: The Sun shines by turning some of its mass into light
A balloon gets lighter when you let the air out
items.why: The Sun turns about 4 million tonnes of its mass into energy every second. Picking the balloon is a good thought, but the balloon just loses air, which is matter. No mass turns into energy there.

items.p: Einstein's famous rule linking mass and energy is E = m____.
items.why: E = mc². E is energy, m is mass, and c is the speed of light. Because c is huge, a little mass holds a huge amount of energy.

items.p: Most of the mass of your body comes from…
opts: the energy of tiny quarks moving inside your atoms
items.why: Inside the protons and neutrons of your atoms, quarks move about with enormous energy, held together by a very strong force. That energy makes up most of your mass. Picking the Higgs field is close: it gives the tiny particles their own small masses. But that is only a small part of the total.

items.p: Scientists know exactly what gravity is and how it works at the tiniest sizes.
items.why: False. Einstein's theory works for planets and stars, but it does not fit with quantum physics, the science of the tiniest things. Some think there is a particle of gravity, the graviton, but nobody has found one.

items.p: Why do astronauts exercise for about two hours every day in the space station?
opts: Without weight to carry, their bones and muscles get weaker
items.why: On Earth, carrying our weight keeps bones and muscles strong. In free fall, they carry nothing, so they weaken. Hip bones can lose about 1 to 1.5 parts in every 100 each month. Picking 'to push the station' is creative, but the station is moved by small engines, not by exercise.

items.p: Satellites called GRACE measured tiny changes in the Earth's pull over north-western India. What did they find?
opts: Underground water was being used up fast
The Earth had stopped spinning there
items.why: Water has mass, so it pulls. When underground water is pumped out, the pull over that area gets very slightly weaker. In 2009, scientists used GRACE to show that groundwater in north-western India was being used up fast. Picking 'a new mountain' is a good guess about mass. But the change was less mass, not more.
items.context: Water has mass, so a lot of water underground pulls a tiny bit on things above it. Two satellites called GRACE could measure tiny changes in the Earth's pull.

items.p: Why can't you stand on Jupiter, even though it pulls harder than the Earth?
opts: It has no solid ground to push back on you
It is too far away to reach
items.why: Jupiter is a giant ball of gas. There is no solid surface to give a support force. You would keep sinking into thicker, hotter gas. Picking 'pushes you away' mixes it up. Jupiter's gravity pulls, just like the Earth's.

items.p: Brahmagupta wrote in 628 CE that the Earth attracts things. Isaac Newton wrote a law of gravity in 1687. Who discovered gravity? Give a reason for your answer.
items.a: Any reasoned answer. For example: Brahmagupta understood that the Earth pulls things. Newton worked out a rule for how strong the pull is, and showed the same pull holds the Moon. So they each discovered a different part.
items.why: There is no single right answer. Good answers say what each person really did.
items.context: Brahmagupta was an Indian astronomer. Isaac Newton was an English scientist who lived about a thousand years later.

items.p: Einstein said his happiest thought was that a person falling from a roof would not feel their own weight. Explain why a falling person feels no weight.
items.a: We feel our weight only through the push of whatever holds us up, like a floor. A falling person has nothing holding them up. So nothing pushes on them, and they feel weightless, even though gravity is still pulling.
items.why: The weight you feel is the support push. In free fall, it is zero.
items.context: In 1907, Albert Einstein was a clerk in the patent office in Bern, in Switzerland, when he had this thought.

items.p: A forcemeter is useless in the space station. Describe one way an astronaut could compare the masses of two things there.
items.a: Tape each one to the end of a ruler over a table edge, twang it and watch the wobbles. The one that wobbles more slowly has more mass. This uses mass, not weight, so it works in space. Real astronauts rock on a chair on a spring.
items.why: Mass makes things hard to get moving, even with no weight. Timing a wobble measures that.
items.context: In the space station, everything is in free fall, so nothing presses on a forcemeter or a scale.

items.p: In the root project, you laid the jar on its side, and the roots bent down. How do scientists think a root tip feels which way is down?
opts: Tiny heavy starch grains sink to the bottom of its cells
The water in the jar tells it
items.why: Most scientists think tiny heavy grains of starch sink to the bottom of root-tip cells, so the cells feel which way is down. Plants with no starch grains still sense down a little, so there may be other ways too. Picking 'the water tells it' is a good idea, because roots do grow towards water too. But in this jar, the roots bent down even with water all round them.
items.context: In the root project, you grew moong seeds in a jar, then laid the jar on its side.

items.p: In 2023, scientists found that antimatter falls upwards.
items.why: False. In 2023, scientists at CERN, near Geneva, dropped atoms of anti-hydrogen. They fell downwards, like ordinary atoms.
items.context: Antimatter is a strange mirror version of the matter we are made of. For many years, nobody knew which way gravity would pull it.

items.p: Lie on your bed for one minute, then sit on a chair for one minute. Write which parts of your body are pushed up in each case. Which feels more restful, and why?
items.a: Lying down, the bed pushes up on my head, back, bottom and legs. Sitting, the chair pushes mostly on my bottom, and the floor on my feet. Lying feels more restful, because the push is spread over much more of me, so no one part is squeezed hard.
items.why: Gravity pulls on every part of you. A support force spread over a big area presses less on each part.

items.p: Draw the space station going round the Earth. Draw an arrow for gravity's pull on it, and an arrow for the way it is moving.
items.a: The gravity arrow points from the station to the centre of the Earth. The movement arrow points sideways, along the circle.
items.why: Gravity pulls the station towards the Earth. Its fast sideways movement means it keeps falling round the Earth and missing.
items.art: A circle for the Earth and a small space station drawn above it, with space for arrows.

opts: The pull of gravity on a thing
How much matter a thing has
quiz.why: Weight is the pull of gravity. Picking 'how much matter' mixes up weight and mass. Mass is the amount of matter. Picking 'how big' is common, but a big balloon weighs very little.
Mass is measured in grams and kilograms. Picking newtons mixes mass up with weight. Weight is a force, measured in newtons.

quiz.p: On Earth, about what does a 500 gram packet of dal read on a forcemeter?
quiz.why: Every 100 grams weighs about 1 newton, so 500 grams weighs about 5 newtons. Picking 500 usually means reading grams as newtons. Picking 50 usually means getting the pattern 10 times too big.
quiz.context: A forcemeter is a spring tool that measures weight in newtons. You hang a thing on its hook and read the pointer.

quiz.p: Look at the forcemeter. What is the weight of the bag hanging on it?
quiz.why: The pointer is on 6, and a forcemeter measures in newtons. So the bag weighs 6 newtons. Picking 6 kilograms mixes up the units. Kilograms measure mass, not pull.
quiz.context: A forcemeter is a spring tool that measures weight in newtons. You hang a thing on its hook and read the pointer.

chart.title: A forcemeter, measuring in newtons (N)
chart.label: The bag hangs still. Read the pointer.

quiz.p: What does a bathroom scale really measure?
opts: How hard you press down on it
How hard gravity pulls you, directly
quiz.why: A scale feels how hard you press on it, and pushes back just as hard. When you stand still, that equals your weight. Picking 'gravity directly' is very common. But in a lift or a pool, the scale's number changes while gravity does not.

quiz.p: Why don't you sink through the floor?
opts: The floor's atoms push your atoms away
quiz.why: Electrons on the outside of the floor's atoms push away the electrons of your feet. That is the support force. Picking 'air holds you up' usually means thinking air is strong. Air pushes back only a little.

quiz.p: A stone reads 3 newtons in the air and 2 newtons under water. Why?
opts: The water pushes up on it
quiz.why: Water pushes up on the stone, so the spring holds less. Lift it out and it reads 3 again. Picking 'gravity is weaker in water' is the most common idea. Gravity is just the same.
quiz.context: A forcemeter is a spring tool that measures weight in newtons. You hang a thing on its hook and read the pointer.

chart.title: Made-up example: a stone on a forcemeter, in air and in water
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what results can look like. Your numbers will be different.

quiz.p: A lift starts going up. How do you feel?
quiz.why: To start you moving up, the floor must push you harder than usual. You feel that extra push as being heavier. Picking 'lighter' usually mixes up starting up with slowing down at the top.
quiz.context: This question is about a lift, a small room that carries people up and down a building.

quiz.p: A leaky bottle of water is dropped. While it falls…
quiz.why: The water and the bottle fall together, so the water does not press on the bottle. It stops squirting. Picking 'faster' usually means thinking falling makes things heavier.
quiz.context: In the Drop It experiment, you dropped a bottle with holes in it while water was squirting out.

quiz.p: Astronauts float in the space station because…
opts: they and the station are falling round the Earth together
there is no gravity up there
quiz.why: Gravity at the station is about 90 out of every 100 parts as strong as on the ground. They float because they are falling together, so nothing pushes on them. Picking 'no gravity' is the most common mix-up of all.

quiz.p: About how strong is the Earth's gravity at the height of the space station, compared with on the ground?
quiz.why: The station is only about 400 kilometres up, which is close, compared with the size of the Earth. Gravity there is almost as strong as on the ground. Picking zero means believing the 'no gravity in space' idea.

quiz.p: A child has a mass of 30 kilograms on Earth. What is her mass on the Moon?
quiz.why: Mass is how much matter she is made of, and she brings all of it to the Moon. So her mass is still 30 kilograms. Her weight is about one sixth. Picking 5 kilograms mixes up mass and weight.

chart.title: The weight of a child with a mass of 30 kilograms, in different places
chart.note: The child's mass is 30 kilograms everywhere. Only the pull changes. The Sun and Jupiter have no ground to stand on, so these are 'if you could stand there' numbers.

quiz.context: This question is about mass and weight on the Moon. The Moon pulls about one sixth as hard as the Earth.

quiz.p: Light has no mass. Does gravity bend its path?
opts: Yes, because light carries energy, and gravity works on energy
No, gravity only pulls things with mass
quiz.why: In 1919, astronomers saw starlight bend as it passed close to the Sun. Gravity works on energy, and light has energy. Picking 'no' is a sensible guess, because Newton's rule is about masses pulling masses.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists still NOT know?
opts: What gravity really is at the tiniest sizes
Whether things weigh less on the Moon
quiz.why: Einstein's theory of gravity does not fit with quantum physics, the science of the tiniest things. Nobody knows how to join them, or whether the graviton exists. The other two are well known and easy to see.

quiz.p: Stars at the edges of galaxies move too fast for the mass we can see. What do most scientists think?
opts: There is unseen mass, called dark matter, pulling them
Gravity does not work in galaxies
quiz.why: Most scientists think there is invisible dark matter whose gravity pulls the stars. Nobody has caught a particle of it, and some scientists think gravity's rules need changing instead. Picking 'gravity does not work' goes too far. Gravity works, but something is missing from our sums.
quiz.context: Vera Rubin, an American astronomer, measured how fast stars move at the edges of spiral galaxies, in the 1970s.

applications: Shops and markets weigh rice, dal, vegetables and gold on scales that are checked by government inspectors, so that buyers are not cheated.
Doctors weigh babies and children at every check-up, to see that they are growing well.
Lifts, bridges and buildings are designed to hold far more weight than they will ever carry, to stay safe.
Trucks are weighed on big weighbridges at highway toll plazas, so overloaded trucks do not damage roads and bridges.
Aircraft crews add up the weight of passengers, bags and fuel before every flight.
Ships, boats and life jackets float because water pushes up on them. Life jackets are designed to keep your head above water.
Astronauts train for weightlessness in huge swimming pools and on aircraft that dive along a curved path, so everyone inside falls together for about 20 seconds.
Space agencies, like ISRO, work out the weight of every rocket and satellite, so the engines are strong enough to lift them.
Satellites like GRACE measure tiny changes in the Earth's pull to track underground water, melting ice and the shapes of mountains.
GPS in phones uses a very exact model of the Earth's shape and gravity, built on work by mathematicians like Gladys West.
Weightlifters and gymnasts train to carry and balance their weight, and astronauts exercise daily to keep their bones strong.
Nuclear power stations, like those at Tarapur and Kudankulam, turn a tiny bit of mass into a lot of energy, as Einstein's rule E = mc² says.

open_questions.why_open: Einstein's theory of curved space and time works beautifully for planets and stars. But it does not fit with quantum physics, the science of the tiniest things. Nobody yet knows how to join them.

open_questions.q: Does the graviton, a tiny particle that carries gravity, exist?
open_questions.why_open: Many physicists think it should. But gravity is so weak that nobody has any idea how to catch a single graviton.
A small fridge magnet can hold up a paper clip against the pull of the whole Earth. Gravity is far weaker than the other forces we know, and nobody can explain why.

open_questions.q: Why do the mass that gravity pulls on and the mass that makes things hard to push always match exactly?
open_questions.why_open: Every test, including a satellite called MICROSCOPE that finished in 2022, finds them equal. Einstein built his theory on it, but nobody knows why it is true.

open_questions.q: What gives each tiny particle the exact mass it has?
open_questions.why_open: The Higgs field gives electrons and quarks their masses, but nobody knows why those masses have the values they do.
Gravity tells us there is about five times more unseen matter than ordinary matter. Nobody has ever caught a particle of it. A few scientists think gravity's rules need changing instead.

open_questions.q: Why do careful measurements of the strength of gravity not quite agree?
open_questions.why_open: Different laboratories measure the gravity constant, called big G, and get slightly different answers. Nobody knows if the cause is hidden mistakes, or something new.

open_questions.q: How exactly do plants feel which way is down?
open_questions.why_open: Sinking starch grains are the main idea, but plants without them still sense down. Scientists are still searching for all the sensors.

open_questions.q: Could people live for years on Mars or the Moon, with less weight?
open_questions.why_open: We know what happens to bones and muscles in free fall. Nobody knows yet what living for years with one third, or one sixth, of our weight would do to a body.

Why do you feel so light in a pool, and so heavy when you climb out?
When a ball falls, has its weight gone? What has changed?
Is the space station falling right now? Why doesn't it land?
Can you feel gravity itself, or only the floor pushing back?

Who in our family has gravitas? What makes you say so?
Which do you think is heavier, a kilogram of cotton or a kilogram of iron?

maths.problem: In the kilogram experiment, 100 grams of rice weighed 1 newton. How much would 800 grams weigh? And a 2 kilogram bag of atta?
maths.answer: 800 grams weighs about 8 newtons. 2 kilograms weighs about 20 newtons.
maths.explain: Every 100 grams weighs about 1 newton. 800 grams is 8 lots of 100 grams. So it weighs 8 × 1 = 8 newtons. 2 kilograms is 2,000 grams, which is 20 lots of 100 grams. So it weighs about 20 newtons.
maths.context: In the kilogram experiment, you weighed bags of rice on a kitchen scale in grams. Then you hung them on a forcemeter to read their weight in newtons.

chart.title: Made-up example: the weight of bags of rice on a forcemeter
chart.note: Each extra 100 grams adds about 1 newton. A whole kilogram, 1,000 grams, weighs about 10 newtons.

maths.why_maths: Once you know the pattern of 1 newton for every 100 grams, you can work out any weight without hanging it up. That is how a pattern becomes a rule.

maths.problem: Look at the forcemeter in the picture. The big numbers are whole newtons. Each small mark is half a newton. What does the stone weigh?
maths.explain: The pointer is past the 2 but before the 3. It sits on the small mark halfway between them. Each small mark is half a newton. So the reading is 2 and a half newtons.
maths.context: In the stone experiment, you hung a stone from a forcemeter and lowered it halfway into a bucket of water. A forcemeter is a spring tool that measures weight in newtons. You hang a thing on its hook and read the pointer.

chart.title: A forcemeter holding a stone half in water
chart.label: Each small mark is half a newton.

maths.why_maths: A forcemeter is only useful if you can read the marks between the numbers. Reading half-marks lets you see small changes, like the water's push.

maths.problem: The stone read 3 newtons in the air and 2 newtons fully under water. Resting on the bottom, with the string slack, it read zero. How hard was the water pushing up? How hard was the bucket's floor pushing up?
maths.answer: The water pushed up with 1 newton. The bucket's floor pushed up with 2 newtons.
maths.explain: In the air, the spring held all 3 newtons. Under water it held only 2. So the water held 3 − 2 = 1 newton. On the bottom, the spring held nothing. The water still held 1 newton. So the floor held the rest: 3 − 1 = 2 newtons. Check: 1 + 2 = 3.
maths.context: In the stone experiment, you weighed a stone in the air, fully under water, and resting on the bottom of the bucket.

chart.title: Made-up example: a stone on a forcemeter, in air and in water
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what results can look like. Your numbers will be different.

maths.why_maths: Subtracting the readings shows how the job of holding up the stone was shared between the spring, the water and the floor. The total always stays 3 newtons, because gravity's pull does not change.

maths.problem: A child has a mass of 30 kilograms. On Earth, she weighs about 300 newtons. The Moon pulls one sixth as hard. What does she weigh on the Moon?
maths.explain: One sixth means sharing into 6 equal parts and taking one. 300 divided by 6 is 50. So on the Moon she weighs about 50 newtons. Her mass is still 30 kilograms.
maths.context: In the Pull Cards game, the Moon card says your weight there is about one sixth of your weight on Earth.

chart.title: The weight of a child with a mass of 30 kilograms, in different places
chart.note: The child's mass is 30 kilograms everywhere. Only the pull changes. The Sun and Jupiter have no ground to stand on, so these are 'if you could stand there' numbers.

maths.why_maths: Dividing by 6 turns 'the Moon pulls one sixth as hard' into a real number you can compare with your Earth weight.

maths.problem: In the lift experiment, a 1 kilogram bag read 10 newtons standing still, 11 newtons as the lift started up, and 9 newtons as it slowed at the top. Draw a bar chart of the three readings. How much more did it read starting up than slowing down?
maths.answer: 2 newtons more. Here is the bar chart.
maths.explain: Draw one bar for each moment: 10, 11 and 9 newtons. Starting up it read 11. Slowing down it read 9. 11 − 9 = 2. So it read 2 newtons more starting up. The bag never changed. Only the spring's pull changed, while the lift sped up or slowed down.
maths.context: In the lift experiment, you hung a bag on a forcemeter during a lift ride and wrote down the readings at different moments.

answer_chart.title: A 1 kilogram bag on a forcemeter in a lift

maths.why_maths: The changes in a lift are small, often only about a newton. Bars side by side make a small difference easy to see.

maths.problem: The space station goes round the Earth about 15 times a day. Each trip round is about 40,000 kilometres. About how far does it travel in one day?
maths.explain: 15 trips of 40,000 kilometres is 15 × 40,000. First do 15 × 4 = 60. Then add the four zeros: 600,000. So it travels about 600,000 kilometres a day. That is more than the distance from the Earth to the Moon and halfway back again! The real trip is a little longer, because the station flies above the ground.
maths.context: The International Space Station is always falling round the Earth, but it moves sideways so fast that it keeps missing. That is why astronauts inside float.

answer_chart.title: How far the space station travels as the trips add up

maths.why_maths: Multiplying the trips by the distance of each one shows just how fast the station must move sideways to keep falling and missing the Earth.

roots.context: We have found that weight is the pull of gravity, and that a falling bottle stops leaking even though gravity still pulls it. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: A falling bottle stops leaking, though the Earth pulls it as hard as ever. Gravity pulls every part of you along together, so your body has no way to sense it. What you feel as heaviness is the push of whatever holds you up. So when you feel your weight, you are really feeling the ground pushing up.
deep_truth.habit: We think the heavy feeling in our body is gravity itself. But a falling child is pulled just as hard and feels no weight at all. The heaviness was the push of the floor all along.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Drop It experiment, the leaking bottle stopped leaking while it fell, and the coins stopped stretching their rubber band. Astronauts, who are falling all the time, feel weightless, though gravity at their station is about 90 out of every 100 parts as strong as on the ground.

three.who_am_i: You feel heavy only because something holds you up. With nothing holding you, you would feel no weight, and still be all of you.
three.what_is_life: Bones grow strong because they carry weight every day. In space, with nothing pressing on them, astronauts' bones get weaker.
three.what_is_this_world: Everything pulls on everything else, all the time. You pull on the Earth, and the Earth pulls on you.

roots.thread: Your weight is not one pull from somewhere under your feet. Every particle of the Earth attracts every particle of you, and you attract each of them back. Your weight is all those pulls added together. This shows that nothing stands alone. Even being heavy is something you and the whole Earth do together.

teachings.teaching: Nothing has its nature all by itself. Everything is what it is because of the other things it depends on.
teachings.link: Heaviness is like this. You feel heavy only when the Earth pulls you and something holds you up. Take away the floor, as in a fall, and the heavy feeling is gone, though you have not changed.

science.text: A person falling freely feels no weight, though gravity pulls as hard as ever. Einstein called this his happiest thought, in 1907, and built his theory of gravity on it.

how_we_found_out.story: In the 1600s, people believed that a thing weighs exactly the same everywhere on Earth. Some even hoped to use a swinging pendulum as a measure that every country could share, because it should swing the same everywhere. A pendulum is a weight on a string or a rod, swinging back and forth. In 1672, the French astronomer Jean Richer sailed to Cayenne, in South America, close to the equator. His pendulum clock had kept good time in Paris. In Cayenne it ran slow, losing about two and a half minutes every day. To make it keep time, he had to shorten the pendulum. A pendulum swings more slowly when gravity pulls it more weakly. So the Earth was pulling a little more weakly near the equator. In 1687, Isaac Newton explained why. The Earth spins, so it bulges at the equator, and the spin also flings things outwards a little. Both make things weigh slightly less there. From the 1730s, expeditions to Lapland and to Peru measured the Earth's shape, and showed that Newton was right.
how_we_found_out.who: Jean Richer, a French astronomer, and Isaac Newton
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: A thing weighs exactly the same everywhere on Earth. Richer's pendulum clock ran slow near the equator, which showed that gravity pulls a little more weakly there.
